One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1316. Lazio lose Nuno Tavares and Sutalo for at least 3 weeks to fresh injury

Serie A leaders Lazio will be without both Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo for at least three weeks after tests showed muscular lesions.

The pair both sustained injuries during the 1-1 draw with Napoli at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona on Sunday.

This caused them to withdraw from international duty in the Nations League for Portugal and Croatia respectively.

According to Sky Sport Italia, the tests have now shown the extent of the damage, and both suffered muscular lesions.

That means both Nuno Tavares and Sutalo are expected to be out of action for at least a period of three weeks.

The full-back and central defender should therefore miss the upcoming Serie A fixtures against Lecce and Torino, but hope to be available for coach Gennaro Gattuso in the first week of December.

Sutalo has made eight Serie A appearances for the Biancocelesti since his loan with option to buy from Ajax on August 22.

Nuno Tavares contributed a goal and four assists in 11 Serie A games so far this season, but has a long history of muscular injuries.

England manager Thomas Tuchel has admitted that the Premier League’s financial strength can make it difficult for young English players to break through, but insists there are still several pathways to the highest level.

Speaking ahead of England’s UEFA Nations League clash with Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, Tuchel was asked by GIVEMESPORT reporter Sam Cohen, whether the Premier League’s ability to recruit established international stars was making it increasingly difficult for homegrown players to secure regular first-team opportunities.

The question came following Jobe Bellingham’s first senior England call-up, with the midfielder having continued his development in Germany with Borussia Dortmund.

Tuchel, who previously managed Borussia Dortmund and Bayern Munich, acknowledged the potential difficulties but stressed that every player’s journey is different.

“Yes and no, it can be, but I think everyone has to find his own way,” Tuchel explained.

“I think there are enough examples where you go through the pathway and you find your way, and you’re at the right moment, in the right club, with the right coach, and things just fall your way.”

The England boss also highlighted the importance of timing and opportunity, suggesting that factors outside a young player’s control can have a significant influence on their development.

Don’t forget, you also need a lot of luck, sometimes an injury from an established player, sometimes a coach that just trusts you or knows you from the pathway.

“There are so many different ways to make it to the top, and so few players really make it.”

Bellingham has followed a similar route to his older brother Jude, who also left English football to develop at Dortmund before establishing himself as one of Europe’s leading midfielders.

Tuchel believes the environment at the Bundesliga club provides an excellent platform for young players to develop under pressure.

“Jobe went a bit of a similar way, like Jude, and went abroad and got his next step of development in the Bundesliga, in a very emotional, proper football club like Dortmund, where you’re under pressure to perform.

“To perform for the club and for the city means a lot, and they play with a lot of pride. So it’s a good school, a good school of development and his way.”

The England manager was also full of praise for Bellingham’s progress through the international youth setup, revealing that the midfielder has already impressed during his first senior training sessions.

Jobe Bellingham record for Borussia Dortmund

He said: “Jobe deserves to be here because he had an excellent spell over a long period of time with the U21s as a captain, and with Dortmund he played a strong season.

“You could see it, he had two good training sessions already. So it’s good to have him, good to see him.”

Tuchel’s comments underline his belief that there is no single route to international football, with Bellingham’s move abroad demonstrating how young English players can establish themselves outside the Premier League.

#1314. Italian Media Cast Verdict on England Ace John Stones at Inter

There can be little doubting the quality of John Stones, one of the greatest defenders in Premier League history. After all, the Englishman lifted six top-flight titles with Manchester City before moving to Inter Milan this summer.

The 32-year-old arrived in Italy with a wealth of experience, having played 94 international matches for England. Add to that his Champions League final win in 2023 – coincidentally against Inter – and it looked like a great signing for the Serie A side.

However, only months into his spell abroad, it doesn't seem as though things are going so well for Stones.

Making £120,552 per week, Stones is the eighth-best-paid overseas Englishman right now, and there was much anticipation for his debut at Inter. The centre-back made his first appearance in pre-season against Real Betis, coming on for 20 minutes. That first showing had new fans excited, as they hyped up his ball-playing skills.

He actually scored the winner in that 1-0 victory, earning praise from Italian media outlet Gazzetta dello Sport, who handed the debutant a 7/10 rating for his short cameo, noting: "The timing and punctuality are English—a goal on his debut, without wasting a second—but what's most striking is the coordination of a seasoned striker."

When the season proper started, Stones made his official debut in Serie A, coming off the bench again for the 4-1 opening round win over Monza. Since then, though, he's played just three more times in all competitions – including in the loss against Real Madrid in the Champions League – starting just once.

The issue is familiar to anyone who has followed Stones in the past few years of his career. Indeed, injuries are to blame for his lack of game time.

An increasing number of footballers are playing with holes cut in their socks - here's why.

Stones has been sidelined with a hamstring strain since September, only just returning to the bench last weekend, as he was an unused sub in the 2-0 win over Como. Amid the fitness concerns, the Italian press are starting to express their doubts.

In an eye-opening update, it's now been suggested that the Englishman could be replaced at Inter in the January transfer market. Gazzetta dello Sport ask the damning question: 'What has happened to Stones?'

The article then claims he's 'under scrutiny' and states that if his fitness doesn't improve, his position in the team could be at risk when the winter window opens. The report adds:

"Various physical issues hang over him. In the last five years he has never managed more than 25 appearances in the Premier League: 14, 23, 16, 11 and just 9 last season. For now, he is stuck on three [in Serie A]."

Stones has not been called into Thomas Tuchel's squad for the November international break to face Croatia and Spain. As such, he can use the next few weeks to get himself up to full fitness, with Inter facing Atalanta on 22 November in their next match.

There are nine games in total for the Italian club until the January transfer market opens. It appears as though Stones has until then to cement his status in the team as a reliable option for Cristian Chivu.

#1313. Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. At present, the only unequivocally documented >3.9-Gyr-old rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada1,2,3. Here we report a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, in which primary magmatic zircon records elevated δ18O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive εHf(t) values (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27). This suggests a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the roughly 4.0-Gyr-old Idiwhaa unit in Acasta2, the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin4. Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrate that its parental magma formed by means of low-degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface-altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.

a, Geological map of the early Precambrian rocks in the North China Craton94, showing the distribution of Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic rocks. b, Geological map of the Qian’an-Lulong area (modified after refs. 95,96,97), showing the spatial distribution of the early Archaean Muchangkou–Shimen Complex, which includes the Muchangkou Complex in the Huangbaiyu area and the Shimen Complex in the Labashan area16. c, Geological map of the Shimen Complex16. The complex is composed of Eoarchaean to Mesoarchaean granitoids and supracrustal rocks as enclaves of varying sizes in undeformed 2.5-Gyr-old potassic granite.

a, View of the hill showing the outcrop location of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss. b, The 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss is aligned parallel to the foliation in the 3.5-Gyr-old potassic granite gneiss and is intruded by 2.5-Gyr-old undeformed potassic granite. The locations of samples J2212, J2302 and J2303 are shown. c, 3.95-Gyr-old banded trondhjemitic gneiss (J2212). The light-coloured layers, commonly less than 1 cm in width, are considered to be deformed granitic veins. d, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2302). e, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2303). Compared with sample J2212, there are fewer veins in J2302 and J2303 and these were removed during sample preparation. f, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2302) shows a granoblastic texture and is composed of plagioclase, quartz and biotite, with minor microcline. g, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2303) has a similar texture and mineral composition to J2302, except for containing less biotite. h, 3.95-Gyr-old banded trondhjemitic gneiss (J2212) consists of different components. The lower right contains more K-feldspar (monzogranitic layer) compared with the upper left (trondhjemitic layer), consistent with the banded characteristics in the field. Both layers show the same foliation defined by oriented biotite flakes.

a, 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (J2302). b, Trondhjemitic gneiss (J2303). c, Banded trondhjemitic gneiss (J2212, including zircons analysed in two sessions from the same sample, marked as J2212A and J2212B). On the left are CL images and on the right are secondary electron images. MA and RC identify magmatic and recrystallized domains, respectively, whereas R represents overgrowth rims and grains newly formed during metamorphism. The analytical sites are marked with white circles, together with the analysis number and age. Secondary electron images show that the weakly modified zircons retain euhedral prismatic shapes, a typical characteristic of magmatic zircon. This feature is particularly evident in zircons from sample J2303, which have been less affected by metamorphism.

a, Zircon analyses of trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2302 define two concordant age groups at 3.95 Gyr and 3.45 Gyr, interpreted as the timing of magmatic crystallization and subsequent metamorphism, respectively. b, Most zircons in trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2303 are magmatic and cluster near 3.95 Gyr. Overgrowth rims show radiogenic Pb loss, including analysis 61.1R, which is the closest to concordia. c, Zircon analyses from banded trondhjemitic gneiss sample J2212 (including zircons analysed in two sessions from the same sample, marked as J2212A and J2212B) are more scattered, with the main population along a discordia line from 3.95 Gyr. However, several zircons with magmatic zoning yield concordant ages of 3.86–3.70 Gyr, potentially owing to the intrusion of thin granitic veins and/or partial resetting of the U–Pb system of 3.95-Gyr-old zircons. Analysis 63.1MA in J2212B has the oldest 207Pb/206Pb age of 3,989 ± 10 Myr but shows slightly reverse discordance, probably because of local enrichment of radiogenic Pb during later metamorphism98. d, Concordia diagram of all samples for analyses with <20% discordance. The weighted mean 207Pb/206Pb age of 3,951 ± 3 Myr (95% confidence level, MSWD = 1.15, n = 33) for magmatic/recrystallized cores is considered the best estimate for the magmatic crystallization age of the trondhjemitic gneiss protolith.

Zircon Lu–Hf isotope analyses were carried out in two sessions. Circles and triangles represent the results of the first analyses and squares represent the results of the second analytical session. All of the magmatic/recrystallized zircons with >3.9-Gyr 207Pb/206Pb age have homogeneous 176Hf/177Hf ratios except for J2302-2.1MA, which has a high 176Lu/177Hf ratio. The magmatic/recrystallized zircons with <3.9-Gyr 207Pb/206Pb age in samples J2302 and J2303 are all located near the Pb loss line. Some newly formed zircons have much higher 176Hf/177Hf ratios, which may be related to external fluids introduced during metamorphism.

a–c, REE patterns of zircons from the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (samples J2302, J2303 and J2212, respectively). The REE data were filtered using the methods suggested in ref. 26. d,e, Magmatic oxygen fugacity and H2O content of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss. The oxygen fugacity (fO2) was calculated using the oxybarometer proposed in ref. 82 based on the average REE content of the filtered magmatic zircons. The magmatic water content was calculated using the hygrometer established in ref. 26 and the effect of U loss in the whole rock was corrected assuming a Th/U ratio of 5 (ref. 26). Considering that the composition of sample J2212 may have been influenced by alteration and the intrusion of thin younger veins, the average composition of J2302 and J2303 was used for calculating the fO2 and water content of J2212.

a, An–Ab–Or diagram99. Note that sample J2212 plots in the granite field owing to the presence of thin younger granitic veins. The homogeneous 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss (samples J2302 and J2303) is similar to the granitoids in Anshan and Nuvvuagittuq (mainly trondhjemitic gneiss) but different from those in Acasta, Tarim and Greenland (mainly tonalitic and granodioritic gneisses). b, Nb versus Ta diagram. c, Sr versus Y diagram. and d, La/Yb versus Yb classification diagrams for high-pressure, medium-pressure and low-pressure TTGs4. The 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss consistently plots in the high-pressure TTG field, being similar to the 3.72-Gyr-old Aktash gneiss in the Tarim Craton and some TTG rocks in Greenland but different from many other ≥3.8-Gyr-old granitoids around the world, which mostly plot into the medium-pressure and low-pressure TTG fields. Several samples from the literature that plot outside the ranges in b and d are not shown.

a,b, LILE contents of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss and potential source rocks (Supplementary Tables 6 and 7). The dashed red lines represent LILE contents required for the source to produce the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss by 7%, 10%, 20% and 30% melting, assuming that these elements are perfectly incompatible with bulk partition coefficient equal to 0. Considering that the degree of partial melting of a mafic rock source needs to be >7% for melt aggregation to form magma but <30% to match the high SiO2 contents of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss, the LILE contents of the source need to be in the grey shaded area. Because the sources of Eoarchaean TTGs are from mafic rocks, we have compiled the geochemical data of Eoarchaean mafic rocks worldwide (Methods and Supplementary Table 7). Comparing the LILE contents of these mafic rocks with those required to form the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss, the amphibolite group I in Acasta is the most suitable source to use for modelling, consistent with the fact that it is the only mafic rock >3.95 Gyr old. c, P–T pseudosection for the composition of amphibolite group I from Acasta, assuming X(H2O) = 1.5 wt% and Fe3+/(Fe3+ + Fe2+) ratio = 0.1. The dashed white lines represent the wt% of melt.

a–d, The red dot denotes the median sodic TTG composition4, which was assumed as the starting melt composition. Solid black and orange curves represent the effects of fractional crystallization of plagioclase and hornblende, respectively, whereas dashed black and orange curves represent the effects of accumulation of plagioclase and hornblende, respectively. Orange squares show the compositions of the 3.95-Gyr-old high-pressure TTGs from this study. Small dots represent melts produced by partial melting of the Acasta amphibolite group I (Supplementary Table 9), colour-coded by pressure. Comparison shows that plagioclase accumulation and hornblende fractional crystallization can explain the positive Eu and Sr anomalies in our samples (a,b) but they fail to simultaneously reproduce the high (La/Yb)N and (Gd/Yb)N ratios and the high SiO2 contents observed in the rocks (c,d). By contrast, melts formed under high-pressure conditions match well with the main geochemical characteristics of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic samples.

The positive εHf(t) values of magmatic zircons from the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss indicate that its basaltic precursor was young juvenile crust derived from a DMD. Even if the basaltic precursor (assuming 176Lu/177Hf = 0.022) was derived from a 4.5-Gyr-old DMD with a similar 176Lu/177Hf ratio (0.0384) to modern depleted mantle, its extraction time from the mantle could not be earlier than 4.0 Ga (solid blue line). If the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss was formed by partial melting of basalt immediately extracted from a DMD with similar 176Lu/177Hf ratio, then the timing of mantle depletion can be estimated to be about 4.35 Ga (dashed black line). Earlier depletion of the mantle is required if partial melting of a basaltic precursor occurred some time after its extraction from a DMD (dashed blue line) or the degree of depletion in the mantle is less than modern depleted mantle (dashed red line). If the basaltic precursor was derived from a possible ultra-depleted mantle proposed by some researchers100, the depletion can be slightly delayed. Nevertheless, the depletion still needs to be no later than 4.2 Ga even if the 176Lu/177Hf of the ultra-depleted mantle is as high as 0.041 (solid purple line). Therefore, a Hadean DMD is necessary to yield the Hf isotope composition of the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss.

#1312. Sanchez unhurt after high speed crash for Como and Chelsea goalkeeper

Como goalkeeper Robert Sanchez, who is on loan from Chelsea this season, reportedly smashed his Ferrari into the barrier at 70mph on the Nurburgring in Germany, but emerged unscathed.

The 28-year-old was on vacation during the break for international duty and decided to use his downtime to go racing on the legendary track.

According to The Sun newspaper, he completely demolished the Ferrari 488 Challenge Evo on Monday afternoon when going headlong into the barrier at the Caracciola-Karussell corner.

“He was going way too fast on the turn travelling up to 70mph,” a British holidaymaker who witnessed the crash told The Sun.

“He slammed into the corner and the track immediately got red flagged. It’s a banked corner that goes on more than 180 degrees and he clearly had put too much gas on and drove straight into the barrier.

“The front of his Ferrari was completely demolished and parts were sprayed all over the track. I think he just wanted to have a bit of fun for the week.”

Sanchez is on a dry loan from Chelsea, so there does not appear to be an option to make it permanent at the end of the season.

He has only made three Serie A appearances for Como and one in the Champions League, as the club has largely stuck with Jean Butez between the sticks.

Como lost two of the four games played with Sanchez taking the gloves, against Feyenoord and Inter.

#1311. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. Newcastle will be relieved that this game is at St James’ Park, with the club having lost their previous two away fixtures 4-1 against both Coventry and Leeds.

Summer signing Nicolas Jackson has five goals in his previous six games for Aston Villa in all competitions and looks to be brimming with confidence as he leads the line for Unai Emery. The striker dispatched both finishes for his brace against Fenerbahce with unerring composure and will target more goals at St James’ Park.

One of the interesting subplots to this evening’s game will be watching Johan Manzambi playing for Aston Villa.

The Switzerland international’s decision to reject Newcastle in order to sign for Villa helped convince Eddie Howe to quit in the summer.

Having already missed out on Victor Munoz, who decided to join Liverpool at the last moment, losing Manzambi - their first-choice target across the position board - was a blow Howe did not feel he could recover from.

In short, he was not convinced the alternatives would give him the tools to do the job this season. Aladji Bamba, who was signed instead, has not started a game for Newcastle this season and appears to be well down the pecking order in the centre midfield under Howe’s successor Matthias Jaissle.

Manzambi had a slow start to his Villa career because of injury but he was hugely impressive at the World Cup for Switzerland and is expected to become one of the best midfield players in Europe over the next few years. Nobody can say with any degree of confidence that will be the same for Bamba.

#1310. Top Sports Ranked By Average Daily Calorie Intake

Every sport requires a different level of maintenance in terms of nutrition; some are endurance sports, some are skill-based and others combine some combination of the two which ensures calorie intake varies widely.

At the top end of elite sport, the finest details can have the biggest impacts and what goes into an elite athlete's diet has developed into an extreme science the most demanding sports require an exceptional amount of calories per-day for maintenance and training and for match/tournament days.

However, there is a clear trend as to the higher forms on this list — it's centered around power and stamina, which should give away clues as to what will feature. Other factors come into play, such as refuelling mid-race/competition, sodium levels and much more.

Therefore, we've scouted and collated the top 10 calorific-heavy sports, ranked by daily calories consumed which, when compared to the calorie count of the average individual (2,500 kcal for men, 2,000 for women), goes to show what the body needs to perform at the elite level.

Six Premier League first-team players were tracked over a week of doubly labelled water by Liverpool John Moores researchers. They burned 3,566 calories a day and ate 3,186–3,789 on match days, 2,956 on training days.

It all hinges on match schedules, body makeup, position and load. Typically, footballers remain lean and light, boasting few bulging muscles in favour of agility, speed and constant running, which ensures they eat good carbohydrates, proteins and healthy fats — something which is attainable or even managed by healthy, regular gym-going individuals.

Lionel Messi is indisputably the GOAT when it comes to football, winning titles and breaking records wherever he goes, but how does he do it?

An Ironman race (a long-distance triathlon) is the most extreme mismatch in sport. A study of 18 Ironman athletes measured men burning 10,036 calories over the race and taking on 3,940 — finishing roughly 7,000 in the red on the day.

Since the gut cannot absorb anywhere near as much as the legs expend, it is an incredibly difficult task to manage especially since they also have to balance sodium intake too. Kristian Blummenfelt, the Olympic and Ironman champion, burns 7,000–8,500 a day in training and eats 4,900–6,400.

Thirty-one national-team skiers, weighed and recorded under supervision, ate 4,862 calories on a training day and 4,304 on a sprint competition day — the men's figures, from a 2019 study in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism.

Per hour really puts the sport into perspective, as skiers have to eat between 500 and 1,000+ calories per hour. It also varies across the type of flat terrain (500 – 650 calories per hour), hill/skate skiing (700 – 900 calories and racing (1,000–1,300).

Jordan Mazur, the 49ers' coordinator of nutrition, puts lineman requirements at 3,500 to 6,000 calories a day depending on whether a player is holding weight or building it. It varies due to a player's position, body size, and whether they need to build, lose, or maintain mass, with Joe Thomas revealing the amount of calories he had to eat as an offensive lineman.

Requirements are different for NFL skill players (wide receivers, defensive backs, quarterbacks), big skill players (linebackers, tight ends) and linemen (offensive and defensive linemen), with a high focus on carbohydrates and high protein.

This is the highest genuinely measured single-day intake on the list. During the 2025 Western States 100, a world-class runner finishing third in 14 hours 19 minutes took on 6,720 calories mid-race — while burning 16,104, confirmed by and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology.

He finished nearly 10,000 calories down. Whilst it is less dramatic than others on this list, the constant flow of movement over a long period of time drives up the calorie figures. Elite runners target 60g to 90g (and up to 120g with advanced gut training) of carbohydrates per hour using gels, chews, or sports drinks, as well as sodium-focused supplements and drinks to avoid hyponatremia, which leads to illness, passing out and long-term organ issues.

Heavyweight rowing has the highest routine training demand of any Olympic sport. A 2022 study of 14 elite open-class men put their requirement at 6,775 calories a day in a high-volume week, dropping to 4,626 in a taper.

Intake reportedly tracks it — around 6,970 a day for a national squad at peak volume, per two national-team dietitians writing in Current Sports Medicine Reports, though they label that data unpublished. Individual elite training sessions, roughly twice a day of intense on-water rowing, running, and heavy weightlifting, can burn up to 5,000 calories per session block alone.

The foundational study is still Wim Saris's 1989 work at Maastricht, which followed five riders through the Tour de France using doubly labelled water. They averaged 24.7 MJ eaten against 25.4 MJ burned — roughly 5,900 and 6,070 calories a day, sustained for three weeks. Mountain stages push the peak towards 9,000.

It also varies across different parts of races. There's flat/sprint stages (estimated 4,000 to 5,000 calories burned), mountain/hard stages (7,000 to 9,000+) and in-race fueling to consider as well, that amount to 400–500 calories/hour via gels, carb-mix drinks and rice cakes.

Professional sumo wrestlers are famously extremely powerful, and large. The amount of mass and force needed to succeed at the top level is remarkable, and the bulk comes from structure, not volume — and a consistent dose of the famous Japanese stew, chankonabe.

Reports describe them as being in a place of healthy obesity, with caloric intake ranging from approximately 5,000 to 8,000 kcal—and oftentimes exceeding 10,000. They burn incredible amounts due to their intense keiko (training), which can last up to six hours and begins early in the morning, and they typically skip breakfast, train in a fasted state, and then consuming a massive, nutrient-dense meal at midday—allowing for a metabolic cycle that promotes efficient weight gain while supporting muscle development.

Michael Phelps is the reason everyone thinks they know this number, and the number everyone knows is wrong. The 12,000-calorie breakfast that circulated during Beijing was never his figure. He corrected it himself in an interview with Olympics media: "It's just not true. Maybe eight to ten thousand calories per day."

Even corrected, it is enormous — the product of five to six hours in the water, six days a week, in a medium that strips body heat faster than air. Swimming's demand is relentless rather than explosive, and it runs year-round, ensuring that calories are high but the metabolic and muscular workrate ensure they are one of the most muscular-bound athletes out there.

Usain Bolt was in no doubt when naming the true Olympic GOAT between himself and legendary swimmer Michael Phelps.

The number at the top of this list is also the softest. Brian Shaw, four-time World's Strongest Man, walked Men's Journal through a seven-meal day totalling 12,019 calories — 705g of protein, 1,402g of carbohydrate — eaten across roughly 13 hours. "It's constant," he said. "All day long I have to eat, but it's part of the job."

Everything here is self-reported by men with an interest in the legend. Treat it as the ceiling of what's claimed, not what's proven. Eddie Hall, the former World's Strongest Man, claimed he would devour over '12,000 calories a day, sometimes up to 15,000', which perfectly rounds off this list.

#1309. Juventus welcome Conceicao back to full training, Nico Gonzalez to follow

Juventus have Francisco Conceicao back in full training, and hope Nico Gonzalez will fully recover during the break for international duty too, while Kenan Yildiz is closer to a return.

The Bianconeri limped into November with a decimated squad, stretched very thin by their Serie A and Europa League commitments.

Coach Luciano Spalletti was forced to reshuffle his tactics when missing around 10 players at a time, many of them in attack.

The good news from Sky Sport Italia is that Francisco Conceicao returned to full training today, over three weeks since dislocating his shoulder.

The Portugal international therefore hopes to be available for the first Serie A match back from the break against Venezia on Sunday November 22.

Nico Gonzalez is also getting closer to the full training routine following a calf strain in late October.

Andrea Cambiaso is another player hoping to be back after the break for international duty.

Juve will need to wait a while longer for Kenan Yildiz, who underwent surgery for a stress fracture in his foot in late August, but there are hopes he should be available again in December.

This all points to Spalletti having more wide options to choose from, which in turn could prompt the club to look elsewhere for January reinforcements.

Pierre Kalulu, Khephren Thuram, Manuel Locatelli, Kamil Grabara and Aradkiusz Milik are still out of action.

#1308. 'I feel betrayed, misled, in shock. It was a stupid thing for them to do': ANDY WOODMAN relives the moment he was 'brutally' sacked by Bromley - and how his best mate Sir Gareth Southgate helped him cope

Published: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 05:29 EST, 11 November 2026

Every sacked manager has a sob story – but few dismissals have felt as harsh as Bromley’s recent decision to part ways with Andy Woodman.

Pound for pound, no club has outperformed their history, budget and expectations in English football across the last decade as much as Bromley. But after an understandably tricky start in League One – two wins from their first 10 games – Woodman was shown the door.

In his first interview since that decision last month, the 55-year-old tells Daily Mail Sport about feelings of 'betrayal' and 'shock' before making his pitch to future employers. But the most eye-opening part of our candid conversation comes when I ask the man with more than four decades of experience to recall the club he took over in 2021.

‘Look, Bromley is your classic non-League club,’ says Woodman. ‘I mean that with the greatest respect to all non-League clubs and I hate the word “non-League” as I think it should be “League Three”, as they are all professional.

‘But the facilities are non-League, the mentality is non-League. Everything is done day-to-day, hand-to-mouth, every penny counts, every decision that costs money counts, it is run by people’s personal money.

‘It was tough when I started: we had no turnstiles, no club shop, we trained on the pitch because it was astroturf, we had no gym.’

Andy Woodman was sacked as Bromley boss last month despite leading the club to the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season

Woodman with the FA Trophy in 2022. 'Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair,' says the former Bromley boss

Under chairman Robin Stanton-Gleaves, Woodman and Co, Bromley changed this mentality and shot up the pyramid, winning the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season. Two months later, it was all over.

Asked how he feels about the decision, Woodman, who used to coach in the Arsenal academy system, says: ‘Yeah, I feel betrayed. Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair. That’s fine, I get how the football business works.

‘But the bit that didn't sit comfortably with me was the conversations I was having with people at the club or owners, everyone above me… there was no inkling of any of this. I feel misled. I was surprised.

‘One day, we were talking about plans and the way forward and how to get through this sticky little period with players out injured, then the next minute it was a change of direction. Nothing like, “Right, you’ve got three games to turn it round”, none of that, nothing.

‘My record was good there, the owner always said if anyone can churn out results it was myself. Football has no patience. In football, people always forget where they come from. I understand wanting to move forward. It’s disappointing really, that’s the best word I can use. I feel let down.

‘It was just a normal day when they told me. I was going into training, popped across to where the chairman’s office was and then was just told, “We are going to take a change of direction”. It was no more than that, I didn’t try to change the decision or ask why.

‘It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is… I am sure people will read this and think, “You deserve this” and “You deserve that” but what else can you do? There’s no easy way of doing it.

'When you have been told you are sacked, you don’t really want to stick around and have a long conversation. They didn’t give an explanation. They needed results, they said. We lost to Leicester which was not a great result, obviously. But realistically they are Leicester… and we are Bromley.’

'It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is'

Woodman, who used to be the Arsenal youth team goalkeeping coach, says: 'When I left Bromley that day, I just felt in shock to be really honest'

To hammer home that last point: Woodman’s first game was against Wealdstone in April 2021 in the National League at Hayes Lane. On that same weekend, Leicester were hosting soon-to-be champions Manchester City. Oh, and the Foxes won the FA Cup a month later.

‘When I left that day, I just felt in shock to be honest,’ continues Woodman. ‘I felt the next three games were winnable. I had played seven of the top 10 teams, beaten the top team Huddersfield, my goalie was just coming back from injury and some others were coming back.

‘We had two teams in the bottom four and one just outside so I felt it was my best opportunity to get some much-needed results.

‘To take someone out who has been in football 40 years and been in coaching 25 years and then to put (his former assistant) Byron Webster in charge who had just been fresh out of playing and has never done a coaching session… with every respect, it feels unfair to him. It was a stupid thing to do. I found that really strange, they took one point from those three games. It fascinates me.’

Now, with Bromley bottom of League One, Karl Robinson, the former Salford and MK Dons boss, has taken over. Woodman, though, is keen not to sound bitter and will remember his five-and-a-half years at the club with fondness. He says his best memories are taking Bromley into the Football League, playing at Newcastle in the FA Cup and beating ‘Hollywood Netflix club Wrexham’ in the FA Trophy final.

Sir Gareth Southgate remains his best friend, the pair having met as teenagers in the Crystal Palace academy. They took turns in being best man at each other’s wedding and Southgate is godfather of goalkeeper Andy’s son Freddie, who is on Liverpool’s books.

They also co-authored the 2004 book Woody and Nord which chronicles two polar opposite career paths that started at the same level, one going on to play (and later manage) England, the other a journeyman in the lower leagues.

‘Nothing surprises Gareth and I,’ adds Woodman. ‘We have been in the game for 40 years now. You can argue that in his tenure at England, he got them as high as they have ever been in 60 years and it still was not enough. So it doesn’t surprise us. People have to make decisions and they are business-related, only time will tell if it is the right decision but that’s not my problem any more.

Woodman and lifelong friend Sir Gareth Southgate at the release of their 2004 book 'Woody and Nord' which charts two very different careers in football

Southgate is godfather to Woodman's son Freddie, a goalkeeper on Liverpool's books

‘Gareth was very supportive, so was Alan Pardew and the support from the Premier League right down to the National League, there has been no end of messages I have had, which is comforting.

‘That first Saturday after being out, I didn’t want to be watching or listening to the game, I just wanted to get away because that is the worst. I have had two clubs ring me, there are ongoing conversations and I am just making sure it is the right vehicle for me. What I mean by that is I want an owner that is aligned and who thinks they can compete to get out of their league.

‘My record speaks for itself. If you ask most managers how many promotions and trophies they have won, I bet over long careers, they haven’t got many. For me, with the smallest budget in the leagues, we maximised the team and maximised success.

‘To get two promotions and an FA Trophy win against Wrexham, hitting the play-offs four times in five years, that is something I am really proud of. If nothing else, the Bromley supporters and town are grateful.’

England captain Harry Kane has praised Tottenham Hotspur academy graduate Will Lankshear and revealed that he has spoken to one of the striker’s former coaches about his goalscoring ability.

Speaking at England’s pre-match press conference ahead of Thursday’s UEFA Nations League encounter with Croatia, Kane was asked by GIVEMESPORT reporter Sam Cohen whether Lankshear could eventually succeed him as England’s first-choice centre-forward.

Lankshear has attracted attention following his goalscoring performances for Middlesbrough, with the former Tottenham youngster emerging as a potential candidate for future senior international recognition.

Kane, who also developed through Tottenham’s youth system before establishing himself as one of the world’s leading strikers, admitted he had been impressed by the youngster’s progress.

“I wouldn’t say I’ve followed his whole career. Obviously, this season it’s been hard not to hear about him, and he’s done extremely well at Middlesbrough,” Kane explained.

“I’ve spoken to a friend of mine who coached him here at the younger age groups and said that he’s a goalscorer. He knows how to score, he’s in the right place at the right time, he’s a great finisher.

We talk about a striker sometimes as having that goalscoring instinct, and I think he’s one of those players for sure.

Despite his praise, Kane was keen to stress the importance of allowing Lankshear to continue developing without unnecessary expectations.

“He’s still early in his development. I think what he’s doing right now is perfect for him, playing loads of games, scoring goals and getting confident.

“Whether he comes into the senior side, it’s down to Thomas. If he did, I’m sure he would learn loads here, surrounded by the attackers that we have.”

Will Lankshear for Middlesbrough this season

Kane, who was named the 2026 Ballon d’Or winner, also acknowledged the ongoing discussion surrounding who might eventually replace him as England’s number nine, but warned against placing that responsibility on a young player too early.

“It’s not a time to put too much pressure on him. I know there’s a lot of talk about who’s going to replace me when I’m not here anymore, but just let him do what he’s doing. I think it’s great for his development.”

The England captain revealed that he has crossed paths with Lankshear on a couple of occasions during their respective Tottenham careers, although the pair have not spent significant time together.

“I’ve come across him a couple of times, when he first signed here at Tottenham and then again when we played him in pre-season. I haven’t really spent much time with him.”

Kane concluded by expressing his willingness to help the youngster should he eventually receive an England call-up.

“As time goes on, if he continues, I’m sure he’ll be on the right path to get his chance.

“If he does make it into the senior team, it’ll be great to work with him and try and help him develop as a player.”

Kane’s comments provide an encouraging assessment of Lankshear’s potential, while making clear that the striker’s immediate priority should remain regular football and continued development at club level.

#1306. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

Roma and Milan are on high alert after Endrick confessed he doesn’t ‘know what will happen in January’ due to a lack of regular playing time at Real Madrid, but the asking price is over €60m.

The Brazilian talent was a major investment for Real Madrid to poach him from Palmeiras for up to €60m including add-ons in 2024.

However, despite flashes of pure brilliance, the 20-year-old has consistently struggled to get into the starting XI.

“I just want to play, to be happy and help my team-mates,” said Endrick at a press conference while on international duty with Carlo Ancelotti’s Real Madrid.

“To score goals, provide assists, like at Lyon, one of the best things to have happened to me and one of the happiest times I’ve had.

“I don’t know what will happen in January. That’s in God’s hands. I only ask to do what’s best for my career. Whatever happens, happens. I’ll keep my feet on the ground and do my best. Madrid is a wonderful city, but I’ll always do everything I can to advance my career.”

There was a six-month loan spell with Olympique Lyonnais from January to June 2026, which helped Endrick secure his spot in the Brazil squad at the World Cup.

Roma and Milan were the most interested, along with Aston Villa, for a potential loan move over the summer, but Jose Mourinho was determined to keep the youngster in Madrid.

According to The Athletic, Real Madrid are now even less prepared to let him go out on loan, but could be open to a sale for over the €60m invested to purchase him two years ago.

#1303. Crystal Palace will sack Pierre Sage after disastrous 16-game spell - this is how his reign fell apart over late, intense sessions, dinner at the training ground and an unpopular assistant manager

Published: 10:17 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 05:58 EST, 11 November 2026

Crystal Palace players and club chiefs have grown frustrated over Pierre Sage's training methods, Daily Mail Sport can reveal - and the 47-year-old will be sacked having won just two of his first ten Premier League matches.

A 3-1 defeat by Liverpool on Sunday saw Palace drop to bottom of the Premier League for the first time in nine years and proved to be the final straw for club bosses, who will tell the Frenchman his time is up.

Daily Mail Sport understands that while the Palace players got on well with Sage, they were frustrated by his late training sessions – with some not starting until 4pm. The regimented routine required players to stay at the training ground for dinner on the night before matches, with some not returning home until 8pm ahead of a 2pm kick-off the following day.

The club's hierarchy, meanwhile, expressed concerns early in the Frenchman's tenure that he was not doing enough defensive work on the training pitch.

Sage's philosophy was that the best way to defend was having the ball, meaning training sessions focused on running, pressing and possession rather than defensive structure.

But the lack of focus led to a poor defensive record, with Palace conceding 30 goals in 16 matches across all competitions. Defending set-pieces and counter-attacks has been a persistent problem for Sage’s side.

Pierre Sage will become the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season after a dismal spell at Crystal Palace

Palace sit rock bottom of the Premier League after winning just two of their first 10 games

Daily Mail Sport understands many players voiced fears they were being pushed too hard in training, with sessions the day before a game particularly intense. There were also significant concerns about the quality of Sage's backroom staff, with his assistant Jamal Alioui proving especially unpopular among the players.

There has also been considerable turnover among senior executives, with six departures over the past 18 months. Chief financial officer Mitesh Velani is set to add to that number in the coming months. One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that the disruption to the club’s business operations has the hallmarks of a club heading for relegation.

As Palace look to bail themselves out of trouble, Daily Mail Sport understands former Brentford and Tottenham boss Thomas Frank is in pole position to replace Sage, with six-pointers against Hull City and Coventry City following the international break. Sean Dyche also has admirers at Selhurst Park.

Palace chairman Steve Parish first contemplated sacking Sage over his lack of defensive nous in September, but gave him a stay of execution after Palace kept a clean sheet in a spirited performance away at Leeds on the eve of the international break. However, that display proved an anomaly as Palace shipped 19 goals in the following nine games.

Palace have won just once in their last eight matches in all competitions, beating Fulham 1-0 in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

In September, Daily Mail Sport revealed tensions had emerged between Sage and Parish when the latter took a dim view of the decision to drop teenage defender Jaydee Canvot in their defeat by Ipswich Town.

Palace paid French club RC Lens £4million in compensation to appoint Sage in June after he won the French Cup, finished second in Ligue 1 behind Paris Saint-Germain and was named manager of the season last term. It was the first time in 10 years that Palace had paid compensation to appoint a manager.

Palace chairman Steve Parish (right) first contemplated dismissing Sage in September over a lack of defensive nous

Palace players found Sage’s training sessions too intense and struggled to adapt to the late schedule

Succeeding Oliver Glasner, Palace's greatest manager, proved too big a task for the 47-year-old.

Following Palace's loss to Liverpool, Sage insisted the Eagles have been playing better than their league position suggests and pleaded for more time.

'A lot of times I’ve said we deserved better and it was the case again (on Sunday),' said Sage. 'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

‘I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in (me), and if it's not the case, they will take a decision. I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100 per cent involved in what I have to do.

‘We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be OK.’

#1302. Pochettino Already Has His Own Harry Kane Waiting at Man Utd in Fernandes

Mauricio Pochettino is closing in on the Manchester United job after GIVEMESPORT revealed that the two parties have reached an agreement in principle on personal terms.

Now, Man United must pay the Argentine's $10m release clause to prise him away from the USMNT, with an extra fee needed on top to take his coaching staff to Old Trafford too.

While all of this is going on, the Red Devils' hierarchy are still yet to sack Michael Carrick, but the 45-year-old is expected to be dismissed following talks between Omar Berrada, Jason Wilcox and Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco this week.

Berrada and Wilcox have recommended the appointment of Pochettino, who has been out of club football for two-and-a-half years after being sacked by Chelsea in the summer of 2024.

Should Pochettino's appointment be confirmed, there is no doubt that the 54-year-old is taking on a big job at Old Trafford, given how poor the club has been this term.

Expectations were high that the team would continue to build under the leadership of Carrick after they were so impressive in the first half of 2026, but instead they are in the Premier League relegation zone having won just one of their 10 matches this season.

Elsewhere, they were also knocked out of the EFL Cup after losing a 2-0 lead to be beaten 3-2 by Brighton and Hove Albion at the Theatre of Dreams, while they have also lost two of their four fixtures in the Champions League too.

United produced fantastic comebacks in their previous two games against AS Roma and Aston Villa, but it wasn't enough to convince Wilcox or Berrada that Carrick should remain in the dugout for the trip to Liverpool after the international break.

United will hope that Pochettino is at Anfield, and work will immediately begin on how he is going to turn their fortunes around, with seven weeks to go until the January transfer window opens.

Pochettino had great success with the likes of Harry Kane at Tottenham previously, and he actually has his own version of the England captain waiting for him at Old Trafford, and it's not Benjamin Sesko.

Kane was Pochettino's talisman during his time in charge at Spurs, with the England captain scoring more than 30 goals in a season on three occasions under the Argentine's leadership.

Kane has made no secret of the fact that the 54-year-old has had a big influence on his career, which has led to him winning the Ballon d'Or award in recent weeks.

Pochettino may not have someone on Kane's level when it comes strikers waiting for him at Old Trafford, but he does have Bruno Fernandes.

The Portugal international's decline this season has been one of the biggest mysteries of United's drop-off in recent months, but there is no doubting the quality and influence he has on this team, just like Kane had at Tottenham.

United scored 69 Premier League goals last season, and Fernandes either scored or assisted 30 of those, also registering the Premier League record for most assists in a single season.

The 32-year-old has been a shadow of the player he was last term this time around, but he still has six goals and four assists in 14 appearances.

United's record this season when Fernandes didn't score or assist

All of those goals and assists have come in four of those 14 appearances, with the Red Devils failing to win any of the 10 games where he has provided zero.

If Pochettino is going to get United back up the standings in the coming weeks, he needs to build his team around Fernandes and get the Portuguese star back to his best.

If he does, he has proven before that he can be as influential as Kane was in a Tottenham shirt for him.

#1301. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

But beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area showed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

“There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

Carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”

Martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”

The Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

“We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

“It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

“It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

“We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

“It took us a little bit to adjust to it, but I don’t think it was too difficult to adjust. It was more down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.”
