#1292. Calafiori: ‘I feel older than I was’ in revamped Italy, Arsenal star ready for France

Riccardo Calafiori admits he is ‘starting to feel a little older than I was’ in an Italy squad that is skewing towards youth, as the Arsenal man sees ‘positive elements’ for facing France in the Nations League.

It kicks off at San Siro on Thursday at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

This is a head-to-head for the top of Group 1, as France are currently leading on 10 points, followed by Italy with seven and Belgium on six.

The top two both go into the quarter-finals of the Nations League, then hoping to make it into the Final Four, so Sunday’s trip to Brussels is the deciding factor.

“Having a packed stadium tomorrow will help us, but we know who we are up against, so I doubt it is possible for us to snub this test ahead of Sunday,” said Calafiori in his press conference.

“We’ll play our best tomorrow and then can think about the Belgium game.”

While initially Calafiori had been used as a central defender for Italy, the role he also had at Bologna, he has only recently begun to take the left-back spot for the Nazionale as well.

This is in the wake of his Premier League-winning performances in that position for the Arsenal defence.

“There are a lot of young players in this squad, so I am starting to feel a little older than I was,” added the 24-year-old.

“I have relatively little experience with the Nazionale, but in every match I try to inspire my team and be a leader, more through my actions on the field than any words I might use.”

Italy’s Nations League campaign had started with a disastrous 2-0 home defeat to Belgium, the debut on the return of Roberto Mancini to the bench, but it was followed by victories over Turkiye and an impressive 1-1 draw on French soil.

“I always said it was too early to see big changes and the work the coach was doing, but it certainly helps to get positive results,” noted Calafiori.

“It gives us some more confidence, and tomorrow is again an important test. It was tough for us in France, it was important that we come away with heads held high, and we achieved that.

“Tomorrow we are on home turf, the stadium is going to be packed, these are all positive elements that allow us to build more self-belief, albeit aware there is still a lot more work to do.”

There are reports Kylian Mbappé might miss this match through a muscular injury, only the latest setback after losing Marcus Thuram, Pierre Kalulu, Aurelien Tchaouameni, Manu Koné, William Saliba, Jules Koundé, Maxence Lacroix, Ousmane Dembélé, Maghnes Akliouche and Esteban Lepaul.

“I think this is going to be a very complicated match. France have a lot of options available still, so it doesn’t change that much, and we must stay concentrated on ourselves,” assured Calafiori.

“There isn’t much time to prepare tactically and do things that are too different to at club level, so it’s more about determination and heart.”

The Arsenal defender had man-marked Michael Olise in the first meeting, so will he be doing the same again?

“I hope that I will have to do it tomorrow too. It’s always fascinating to face players of this level.”

#1291. USMNT Want Pep Guardiola As Mauricio Pochettino Nears Man Utd Job

GIVEMESPORT understands that Michael Carrick will likely be informed tomorrow (Thursday, 12 November) that he has been sacked from his position as Manchester United head coach. It looks as though Mauricio Pochettino will take over at Old Trafford.

The Argentine has past Premier League experience, having coached London clubs Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur. Pochettino – who has been linked with the role since 2019 – wants the job, and it's understood that terms are now being finalised to bring him back to England.

However, he is currenlty in charge of the United States men's national team and will need to be replaced if a move to Man Utd is completed. With that in mind, it appears as though US soccer are now planning a highly ambitious move.

While Pochettino only signed a new long-term contract with the USMNT after the 2026 World Cup, GMS understands that the deal contains a $10m (£7.4m) release clause. That compensation will leave the US with a fair bit of cash splashing about as they look to hire their next manager.

Landing Pochettino in 2024, off the back of spells at European powerhouses Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain, was seen as highly ambitious at the time, but their next move could top even that.

A blunt verdict from Richard Keys spotlights a high-profile alternative to Mauricio Pochettino as Michael Carrick's replacement.

GMS understands US soccer want Pep Guardiola as their next men's national team coach. The Catalan is among the greatest managers of all time, but is currently out of work, having left Manchester City in the summer.

He spent a decade in England, from 2016 to 2026, winning six Premier League titles and the Champions League. It's worth noting that Guardiola's tenure partially overlapped with the period in which Man City were found to have breached Premier League financial rules (2009 to 2018), which may diminish some of his achievements.

Even so, the 55-year-old remains one of the best managers in world football, having also enjoyed considerable success at past clubs. His Barcelona side, with MLS star Lionel Messi, between 2009 and 2011 is widely regarded as the greatest football team of all time.

It probably bodes well for Man Utd that the USMNT are already weighing up options to replace Pochettino, with that sort of movement suggesting the Argentine's move to Old Trafford will be greenlit in the near future.

However, the US are likely to face one major issue in any pursuit of Guardiola. The iconic manager is currently on a break from football, and it's unclear when he wants to return to the dugout. Italy approached him to take over as their manager earlier in 2026, but were rejected.

At the time, Italian football federation president Giovanni Malago told La Repubblica (Via The Athletic): “Pep was honest. He took a sabbatical, partly for family reasons, but if he’d done anything, he would have done it with us.”

It remains to be seen if Guardiola's stance has softened in the time since.

#1290. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1289. Mancini on unexpected Italy success, France test and ‘giving fans something to cheer’

Roberto Mancini admits few expected Italy to challenge France for top spot in the Nations League group tomorrow, but they hope to ‘give the fans something to cheer’ and break their San Siro hoodoo.

It kicks off at San Siro on Thursday at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

Italy are currently second in the Nations League Group 1 on seven points, as France are on top with 10, while Belgium follow behind on six.

The final matches will see the Azzurri travel to Belgium, while France take on rock bottom Turkiye.

“We are certainly seeking to confirm and improve the previous performances, and seeing as we have seven points and two games left to play, we can qualify too,” said Mancini in his press conference.

“This seems to be a positive and, considering how things started, a little unexpected.”

Mancini’s return to the bench had been a disastrous 2-0 home defeat to Belgium, prompting fears of relegation into Nations League B, but now they are on the cusp of reaching the quarter-finals.

“We had a good game in France, including in those moments when we had to defend, because they are a great team. There were areas where we can improve and we hope to do that tomorrow in order to win the match.”

That 1-1 draw in Paris boosted confidence considerably in the Nations League, and is the only time Zinedine Zidane’s France dropped points.

“It was a difficult match in certain moments, France kept us pinned back and in the second half Gigio rescued us, but tomorrow’s game will be different. We will try to win against one of the best sides in the world.

“Zidane has won almost every match, he knows the players very well, won so much at Real Madrid as a coach too, and I think he will have a great coaching career at international level.”

Playing at San Siro has its own benefits and problems, because Gianluigi Donnarumma has never been able to play here without being jeered ever since walking away from Milan as a free agent, even now he has gone from Paris Saint-Germain to Manchester City.

“Gigio is a great goalkeeper, as well as an extraordinary young man. Aside from what happened years ago, I don’t think he deserves to be jeered. One would hope fans go to the stadium to cheer on the team, and in turn we hope to give them something to cheer about,” noted Mancini.

San Siro is also not a great omen for the Nazionale, who lost their last three matches played here.

“But I won my most recent one here, and it was by no means easy either, against England.”

It is also the home stadium for Inter midfielder Nicolò Barella and Milan forward Alphadjo Cisse, the latter potentially getting his senior Italy debut.

“I am not affected by the fact we are at San Siro, so my decisions will be made regardless of the stadium setting. They are two players coming off good performances, so that is positive for everyone.”

Inter famously play a 3-5-2 formation, so Alessandro Bastoni and Federico Dimarco must adjust for Mancini’s 4-3-3.

“They also played in a four-man defence, it doesn’t take many training sessions to get them at ease there.”

There are reports France could be without Kylian Mbappé due to a hamstring issue that saw him miss training today, while they are already missing Marcus Thuram, Pierre Kalulu, Aurelien Tchaouameni, Manu Koné, William Saliba, Jules Koundé, Maxence Lacroix, Ousmane Dembélé, Maghnes Akliouche and Esteban Lepaul.

“If Michael Olise were to come down with a cold, I wouldn’t mind,” smiled Mancini.

“Plus Mbappé has the Champions League coming up, so I wouldn’t risk him, it’s best if he rests tomorrow…

“All joking aside, it’s good to play against such strong opponents, that is the joy of football. We must give our best, try to win and improve on what we have done so far.

“France have so many good strikers, it’s honestly hard to choose between them.”

Italy have also been forced into changes, as Gianluca Mancini was injured and Nicolò Zaniolo withdrew over a personal matter.

“We have wingers at the moment who are very young and without much experience, but these games are where they can gain some of that, then hopefully in the next six months everyone will have grown and improved.

“We have to call young players so that we can see and get to know them directly, both for the present and with an eye to the future,” explained the coach.

“Everyone wanted young players, and I agreed it seemed right and logical. People complain they never get to play, so we tried to call them up and get to know them. It can make a big difference for a young player to train alongside those with more experience and at a higher level.”

#1288. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

"I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure." Captain Bruno Fernandes gives his immediate reaction to Manchester United's heavy 4-1 defeat to Como 🗣️ 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8bzmLGkRAX

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Even by the standards of this season to date, though, what unfolded here in the rain in Lombardy was shocking to witness.

Como, inspired by the outstanding Nico Paz, were every bit as good as United – who have won just two of 11 games this season – were a pitiful mess.

United, by contrast, were a sorry collection of strangers. It was impossible to discern a game plan. United were sent out in a strange 4-2-4, with Fernandes and Youri Tielemans operating as almost double false nines. Glenn Hoddle said on TNT Sports that it was like United were “playing in chains”.

Neither looked sure of what they were supposed to be doing. There was just a giant hole where the attack should have been. Everything about them was slow, leaden. The confusion was contagious. Everywhere you looked there were players second-guessing themselves, uncertain of their role and position and habitually a yard or two or three off the pace. But was there any excuse for not running, for so little effort?

The space Paz was afforded to curl in a fine finish less than two minutes in was alarming in the extreme. Carrick brought on Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo for the lamentable Mateus Cunha and Andrey Santos at half-time, but United just got worse.

There was not so much as a snip at the heels of the same player when Paz ghosted in from the right flank, running 30 yards deep into the penalty area before again finishing coolly for the third. Ramón had a free header for the fourth.

United enjoy a spell inside the attacking third to close the half, but it’s too late, at least for the first 45 minutes. The referee blows his whistle and we reach half-time with Como a goal to the good.

There are boos at half-time from United’s travelling support.

United send both of their full-backs forward and it gives Cunha the space to get a shot away from just outside of the box, but his curled effort sails over.

There will be one minute of time added on at the end of this half.

That’s a let off for United. Yan Couto, one of two former Manchester City signings in the Como team, carves open the United defence with a lovely pass and Douvikas should have done better with the finish.

Amazing the difference when you have a centre forward prepared to run in behind. Who would have thought it?

Baturina is the latest to threaten Lammens’ goal. His strike from the edge of the box stings the Belgian’s gloves and Douvikas, who attempts to latch on to the rebound, is offside.

Penalty shout for Como! Douvikas is sent through and it looks as though Lammens is in trouble as he sticks out a leg over which the Greek tumbles, but replays show Lammens withdraws his outstretched limb in the nick of time.

There was also an offside in the build-up, so it does not matter anyway.

Milla and Perrone are really pulling the strings in Como’s midfield. The former comes from the Jose Bordalas/Getafe school of football (think Tony Pulis during peak Britannia era) but you would not guess it given the way he manipulates the ball.

This game has entered into something of a holding pattern, with Como retaining possession as United chase shadows, desperately trying to lock off the centre of the park.

Here, Coute inverts, picking up the ball in the inside right channels before spinning in a ball over the top for Douvikas to stride on to, but the Greece forward shanks his shot over the bar.

Thirty four minutes in and the first chants of “attack, attack, attack” can be heard from the United fans. There is currently a giant hole where you would expect United’s strikers to be. It’s so poor.

Lammens does well to get down smartly and keep out a Douvikas effort, speared towards the near post after a sweeping counter attack. The resulting corner fails to threaten United’s defensive unit.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

The detail on United’s passes has been so poor thus far, with Como picking up loose balls all over the pitch.

Penalty shout for Como! Da Cunha, Douvikas and Baturina combine expertly through the middle, trading the ball with cultured one-touch passes. Baturina is felled by Maguire inside United’s box just as he was gearing up to shoot, but neither the referee nor the VAR are minded to intervene. There is a touch, but it does seem very slight.

United have gone with the box midfield once more, with Fernandes rolling inside as a false 9. Como are counteracting United’s movements through Paz dropping in, so Carrick’s men are struggling to take control of the central zones.

Mbeumo bursts towards the by-line but Ramon gets back sharply to divert the ball behind for a corner, which is easily dealt with.

United drop into a deep block, forcing Como to build around the outside. The ball is worked to the adventurous Couto who loses his boot after an overzealous challenge from Cunha and he earns a free-kick for his troubles, but Da Cunha’s delivery fails to beat the first man.

Chance! Da Cunha plays a lovely through-ball into the right channel for Paz to gallop on to and he flashes the ball across the face of goal, but Maguire gets there before Douvikas and the ball is cleared.

United are struggling to string passes together as Paz cuts out a Lammens pass out from the back, but he cannot keep the ball in play.

United need to settle, and here they decide it best to keep hold of the ball for a while. There are a few sideways passes but the ball goes back to Como.

Valle makes a burst down the left and Dalot’s contact results in a foul, but the free-kick is not up to much.

Como 1 Manchester United 0 (Paz) Well, we said he was special! Como work the ball out to the right, with Da Cunha picking out Paz on the edge of the box. Neither of United’s centre-halves are minded to close the Argentine down, and he opens up his body before shaping the ball around Lammens and inside the far post. Golazo.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is important.”

Como finished last season with a stadium that did not meet Uefa’s Champions League ground requirements, so work began immediately to ensure it would be ready for the 2026-27 season.

This included the construction of a new stand, where the old “Curva Como” once stood, which would increase the stadium’s capacity to 12,379, as well as a pitch expansion, instalment of undersoil heating and upgraded media and hospitality sections.

Andrey Santos, one of United’s summer signings, was asked for his thoughts on Lisandro Martínez’s explosive interview in which he took aim at the club’s hierarchy for their strategy in the latest transfer window. The Brazilian said: “We know the comments [of] Licha, but I think now it’s done so we have to move on and focus on tomorrow [Wednesday].

When pressed on whether Martínez had addressed the squad about his remarks, Santos added: “No, no, no. Nothing happened, as you know we are on the same page, so we believe in ourselves, in your team-mates, your coach, your staff, so I think this is the most important.”

Jack Fletcher and Tynan Thompson played for United against Como in the Uefa Youth League earlier in the day and the pair are named among the substitutes. Fletcher played for 71 minutes, and scored, and Thompson the whole game, which United lost 2-1.

It’s happened before where players have played in the Youth League then made the senior bench later in the day although the very youthful bench is a reflection of just how many absentees Carrick has at the moment.

We’d been braced for thunder and lightning and torrential rain in Como today but so far at least the weather has been pretty kind. It’s raining and moody but far from the severe weather warnings forecast. Michael Carrick will hope that is a portent - the start of a clearing of the storm that has engulfed the club this season.

The United manager is missing nine players through injury, illness and suspension so Matthijs de Ligt gets his first outing for 11 months following a serious back injury. Carlos Baleba has dropped to the bench - he’s still working his way back to full fitness after a long spell out himself - so Mason Mount comes into midfield and Amad Diallo makes way for Matheus Cunha.

Cesc Fabregas has done a fine job at Como and will hope to further enhance that burgeoning reputation with an historic win. United desperately need results - it’s two wins in 10 in all competitions - and face Bournemouth on Sunday after this.

I wonder whether Zirkzee is having flashbacks to a certain team-talk delivered by Vincent Kompany...

The last time De Ligt played for Manchester United, Ruben Amorim was still at the helm. A lot has changed since then (or has it?!) and this evening will be the Dutch defender’s first taste of first-team action under Michael Carrick.

There is no place in Fabregas’ starting XI for Robert Sanchez, who is on loan from Chelsea and conceded three against Feyenoord in the last round of Champions League matches.

Emerging talent Nico Paz will be one to watch out for.

Starting XI: Butez; Couto, Ramon, Kempf, Valle; Perrone, Da Cunha, Milla; Paz, Baturina; Douvikas

Substitutes: Ginelli, Sanchez, Smolcic, Kaiki, Dossena, Caqueret, Ricci, Liberali

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of Manchester United’s trip to Como in the Champions League. Under normal circumstances, a visit to the idyllic Lombardy city would be a source of thrill and wonder, but Michael Carrick heads into the eye of a literal and proverbial storm at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia with his team desperately hoping to reverse their fortunes.

Absolutely tipping it down in Como, with 64mm of rain forecast before #MUFC kick-off here tomorrow ☔️ https://t.co/WvI3X8dilh

Two wins – against Ipswich Town and Sabah – in United’s first 10 matches of the season, a public outburst from Lisandro Martínez and accusations of a “toxic culture” at the club have piled pressure on Carrick. And an uninspiring draw at Elland Road on Sunday did little to settle the rising tide of discontent within the United fanbase.

When asked for his team news, the first words that came from the United head coach’s mouth were: “Right, bit of mixed bag to be honest.” That was not a great sign, and Carrick will be without Martínez, Kobbie Mainoo, Luke Shaw, Ayden Heaven, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu, who are injured, while Leny Yoro serves a suspension following his red card against Atlético Madrid.

Like United, the hosts are without a handful of key players, with Moise Kean, Trevoh Chalobah, Assane Diao and Jesus Rodriguez missing from the match-day squad. The abundantly talented Argentine No 10 Nico Paz will feature, however, and he will be keen to showcase his talents in the Champions League.

Como have ascended from Serie B to Europe’s top table in three seasons (and from bankruptcy in nine) under Cesc Fàbregas’ watchful eye. The Spaniard is a minority owner and shareholder of the club, but as head coach he has introduced an incisive, possession-based style of play which contains hints of the managerial greats under whom he played: Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho, Vicente del Bosque, Antonio Conte etc.

#1287. A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1,2,3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2′,3′-cNMPs; 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3′→5′)-guanosine 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling.

Insect pests cause losses to crop production and damage vegetation4,5. During feeding, insects release oral secretions containing proteins and other molecules that can activate or suppress host plant defence6,7,8. Digestive enzymes hydrolyse cellular components to generate nutrients for herbivores. These breakdown products also act as host-derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that activate plant pattern-recognition receptors9,10. Identifying host-derived signalling molecules and their defence activation mechanisms is essential for developing new plant-protection strategies.

T2-family ribonuclease (RNaseT2) proteins, which preferentially cleave single-strand RNAs between purine and uridine residues, are ancient enzymes that are widely distributed across organisms and functional in diverse biological processes2,11. Plant S-RNases, which mediate self-incompatibility, belong to this protein family12. Phytopathogens also secrete nucleases into host tissues13,14. Human lysosomal RNaseT2 generates purine-2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated oligoribonucleotides that are sensed by Toll-like receptor 8 to activate innate immunity2. Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domains of plant intracellular nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors possess enzymatic activities towards oxidized nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and nucleic acids15,16,17,18,19. Plant TIR domains generate second messengers such as 2′-ADPR and pRib-AMP, which promote the formation of EDS1–Phytoalexin Deficient 4 (PAD4)–Activated Disease Resistance 1 (ADR1) complex and trigger disease resistance15,20,21. Activated plant TIR also catalyses the production of ADPr-ATP and di-ADPR, leading to the complex formation of EDS1-Senescence-Associated Gene 101 (SAG101)–N Required Gene 1 (NRG1), inducing plant cell death16,22,23. Plant TIR domains also synthesize 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP (2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP) through nuclease activity. Arabidopsis nudix hydrolase 7 (AtNUDT7) hydrolyses 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and attenuates TIR-mediated cell death when overexpressed in Nicotiana benthamiana3. However, the contribution of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP to EDS1-dependent immunity remains elusive.

Plant glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins (GRPs) encompassing one RNA recognition motif (RRM) at the N terminus and a glycine-rich region (GRR) at the C terminus regulate plant responses to abiotic and biotic stresses24,25. Arabidopsis GRP7 (AtGRP7) has a positive role in immunity, whereas the Pseudomonas syringae effector HopU1 suppresses AtGRP7-mediaed immunity by catalysing ADP-ribosylation of an arginine residue (R49) in the RRM of AtGRP726,27,28. These data indicate that the RRM of GRPs is central to immune function, although the underlying molecular mechanism remains unidentified. Here we report that the rice GRP NIB1 interacts with invading insect T2 RNases (such as NVR1) to promote ribonuclease activity and the production of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p. Binding to the cyclic nucleotides via RMM stimulates NIB1 phase separation to assemble the plant defence machinery in the nucleus.

Nezara viridula (the green stink bug) is a polyphagous hemipteran pest feeding on a wide range of plants, including economically important food, fruit and vegetable crops and Nicotiana species. Populations of N. viridula have recently increased in rice fields. As a piercing-sucking mesophyll feeder (Fig. 1a), N. viridula uses needle-like stylets to puncture developing seeds or young leaves, extract nutrients and inject effectors29. To identify the secretory enzymes, we profiled proteins in its oral secretions using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) and identified 22 putative digestive enzymes, of which 15 were likely to be secretory based on signal peptide prediction (SignalP 3.0 server) and de-redundancy (Blastp) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Transient expression of these proteins in N. benthamiana leaves identified one candidate enzyme that induced severe cell death and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production within 3 days post-agroinfiltration (dpi) (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). This protein shows high sequence similarity to ribonuclease and we named it N. viridula ribonuclease 1 (NVR1).

NVR1 was predicted to have an N-terminal secretory signal peptide and no transmembrane region. Analysis using the protein family database (Pfam) revealed a ribonuclease (RNase) domain (Fig. 1b) that belongs to the RNaseT2 family11. NVR1 was detected both in N. viridula salivary glands and in infested rice plants, suggesting that it is secreted into plant tissues during feeding (Extended Data Fig. 1d). NVR1 exhibited a nucleocytoplasmic distribution pattern (Extended Data Fig. 1e).

H64 and H116 are conserved among T2 RNases from mammals, herbivorous insects, phytopathogenic fungi and plants (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1f). NVR1 cleaved Cy5-labelled Arabidopsis tRNASer (83 nt) in vitro, whereas NVR1(H116A) and NVR1(H64A) mutants showed mild and strong reductions in substrate degradation, respectively, and the double mutant NVR1(H-doub) was almost completely inactivated (Fig. 1d), supporting H64 and H116 as key catalytic residues11. High-resolution mass spectrometry was subsequently used to identify products of the NVR1-catalysed reaction, which showed accumulation of 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP, as well as a dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate with a mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of 675.1072 in positive mode (Fig. 1e,f). Given that preferentially cleavage of single-stranded RNA between purines and uridines by RNaseT2 produces guanosine or adenosine 2′,3′-cyclophosphate termini2, we designed two oligoribonucleotides, (UAGU)5 and (UGAU)5, as substrates to determine the structure of the product. NVR1 exhibited activity towards (UAGU)5—but not towards (UGAU)5—generating a peak at 5.1 min in the extracted ion chromatogram mode that was identical to the dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate peak at m/z 675.1072, suggesting that NVR1 produced 2′,3′-cGMP-terminated AMP (ApG>p). The ApG>p synthetic standard, eluting at 5.1 min with a m/z of 675.1072 in positive mode, aligns with the NVR1 product (Fig. 1f) and matches the tandem mass (MS2) spectrum (Extended Data Fig. 1g). The accumulation of 2′,3′- cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P was rapidly induced in rice leaves within 2 h after insect feeding (Fig. 1g).

The 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p synthase activity of NVR1 was dependent on the two catalytic histidines H64 and H116 (Fig. 1h). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)–mass spectrometry and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) analysis showed that N. benthamiana leaves expressing empty vector or catalytic inactive NVR1 mutants accumulated much less 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than leaves expressing wild-type NVR1 (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 1h). Leaves expressing NVR1 mutants were impaired in inducing plant cell death (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1i). AtNUDT7 hydrolysed 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p (Fig. 1k). Co-expression with AtNUDT7 attenuated cell death activity of NVR1 in N. benthamiana at 3 dpi, with necrosis completed at 6 dpi (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 1j,k). These results indicate that the NVR1 enzymatic activity was causative to plant cell death.

To investigate plant responses to pest RNase, we generated rice NVR1-GFP transgenic plants that overexpress NVR1–GFP (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis revealed that genes associated with biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence were significantly enriched in NVR1-expressing plants (Extended Data Fig. 2c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2d) were upregulated and levels of jasmonic acid and salicylic acid levels increased (Extended Data Fig. 2e). The Cnaphalocrocis medinalis ribonuclease 1 (CMR1), an NVR1 orthologue expressed by Cnaphalocrocis medinalis—a lepidopteran pest of rice—was detected in oral secretions and also produced 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g), congruent with the rice leaf-feeding data (Fig. 1g). Given this functional conservation, we evaluated the resistance of NVR1 transgenic lines to C. medinalis. The larvae gained less weight on NVR1-expressing plants than on controls (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Adult females laid fewer eggs on NVR1 transgenic lines, and larvae preferred feeding on control plants (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j).

NVR1-expressing plants were stunted and produced fewer tillers, phenotypes associated with the growth cost of constitutive defence activation, whereas rice plants expressing catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub) did not upregulate defence genes and grew normally (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). These results demonstrate that heterologous expression of NVR1 in rice elicited defence responses and enhanced plant resistance to insect feeding, and that NVR1 catalytic activity is essential for immune activation.

To uncover the molecular mechanisms underpinning the NVR1-induced plant defence response, we screened plant proteins that could bind to NVR1 by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry (IP–MS). NVR1-interacting RNA-binding protein 1 (NIB1 (Os03t0670700-04), also known as OsGRP330,31) showed a strong interaction signal (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). NIB1 is a GRP composed of an N-terminal RRM and a C-terminal GRR and shares 80% N-terminal sequence identity with AtGRP726,27 (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Microscale thermophoresis (MST) indicated that NIB1 interacted directly with NVR1 in vitro (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3d), and co-immunoprecipitation confirmed the interaction in planta (Fig. 2b).

Split luciferase complementation (SLC) showed that the NIB1 RRM, but not the GRR, interacted with NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 3e), matching the MST data (Fig. 2a). AlphaFold2 predicted the RRM residue R22 as a contact site (Extended Data Fig. 3f), and the NIB1(R22A) mutant abolished the interaction in planta (Extended Data Fig. 3g). NVR1 interacted strongly with NIB1, independently of its catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 3h–j).

Given that NVR1-like secretory T2 ribonucleases are widespread in insects and phytopathogenic fungi (Extended Data Fig. 1f), and GRPs are conserved across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3k), we investigated whether the RNaseT2–GRP interaction is a common phenomenon. We tested secreted RNases T2 from the insect pests C. medinalis (CMR1) and Helicoverpa armigera (HAR1) and the fungal pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae (MOR1). SLC assays demonstrated that the recognition of T2-family RNases by plant GRPs is universal (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m).

Given that GRPs bind RNA fragments27 and NVR1 requires its RNase activity to elicit defence, we investigated the potential binding of NIB1 to the RNaseT2 products. NIB1–GST was incubated with NVR1 products, denatured to extract the bound molecules, and analysed by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Notably, high-intensity signals of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p were observed (Fig. 2c). Structural modelling of NIB1 with ligands identified two adjoining residues in RRM domain loop, R49 and G50 that were responsible for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP recognition (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). R49 is a known RNA-binding site27, whereas G50 contacts both 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP in our model. G14 and W17 serve as additional recognition sites for ApG>p (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). In MST assays with 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, NHS-labelled NIB1 exhibited high binding affinity. Substitution of either residue with alanine (NIB1(R49A) or NIB1(G50A)) markedly reduced the binding affinity, and the NIB1(R49A/G50A/G14A/W17A) (hereafter NIB1(4A)) mutation fully abolished the ApG>p binding (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3d). G14, W17, R49 and G50 are highly conserved in a group of GRPs across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3n), implying a critical role of these residues in ligand recognition. The NIB1(R49A) mutation impaired NIB1 binding to both RNA and 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides, whereas the NIB1(G50A) mutant maintained binding affinity towards FLAGELLIN SENSITIVE2 (FLS2) 3′ untranslated region (UTR) while showing strongly impaired binding to 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Thus, NIB1 employs shared yet distinct recognition mechanisms for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and RNA.

In MST assays using 2′,3′-cAMP as a positive control, NIB1 did not bind 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP or 2′,3′-cGAMP32 (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g). NIB1 exhibited 4-fold and 34-fold weaker binding affinities for 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP, respectively, compared with 2′,3′-cGMP (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4h,i).

NIB1 contains a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Extended Data Fig. 5a) that mediates phase separation33. PONDR predicted a high average disorder score similar to that of AtGRP7 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). In vitro, NIB1–YFP formed droplets that showed fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and fused to form larger droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5c–e). NIB1–YFP signals also recovered after photobleaching in N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 5f).

To determine whether herbivory induces NIB1 condensation in planta, we generated two pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice lines (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Following 6 h of feeding by third-instar C. medinalis larvae, distinct NIB1 nuclear condensates were clearly visualized (Fig. 2f), indicating that this phase separation is a physiologically relevant response to herbivory. Similar to the observations in vitro and in N. benthamiana nuclei, NIB1–YFP condensates in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 nuclei recovered fluorescence after photobleaching (Extended Data Fig. 5h).

We further analysed the interplay between NVR1 catalytic activity and NIB1 condensation. Wild-type NIB1–YFP, but not the C-terminal IDR-truncated NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP, absorbed NVR1–mCherry into the droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). The droplets of purified NIB1–YFP protein with nucleic acid contamination, but not that of nucleic acid-free NIB1–YFP, were enlarged in the presence of NVR1–mCherry, whereas the catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub)–mCherry did not exert such effect (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). NIB1–YFP exhibited nucleoplasmic localization, and NVR1 significantly enhanced its nuclear accumulation, with about 70% of the examined nuclei containing distinct condensates. N-terminal YFP-tagged NIB1 showed a similar localization pattern (Extended Data Fig. 5l–n). Immunoblotting further confirmed that NVR1 promoted nuclear accumulation of NIB1 (Extended Data Fig. 5o). Nuclear condensates were not observed for the NIB1–NVR1(H-doub) or NIB1(ΔIDR)–NVR1 (Fig. 2g), revealing that the RNase activity of NVR1 is crucial for promoting NIB1 phase separation in the nucleus. In subsequent analyses, we focused on nuclear NIB1 condensates.

Multivalent interactions drive phase separation and locally concentrate molecules, as in dsDNA-dependent cGAS activation and NAD+/ATP-dependent plant TIR activation32,34. We investigated whether 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p would induce NIB1 phase separation. The NIB1(R49A)–YFP and NIB1(G50A)–YFP droplets were smaller than NIB1–YFP droplets with or without NVR1–mCherry (Extended Data Fig. 6a). When co-expressed with NVR1 in N. benthamiana, NIB1(R49A), NIB1(G50A) and NIB1(4A) did not generate sparkling nuclear condensates (Extended Data Fig. 6b), implying that NIB1 phase separation involves binding of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p. Congruently, 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p (2 nM each) promoted NIB1 phase separation in vitro (Fig. 2h and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d), and treatment with 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP or ApG>p increased nuclear condensates in N. benthamiana cells (Fig. 2i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6e). Notably, exogenous application of 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p for 6 h induced distinct nuclear condensates in the pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice plant (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 6f), indicating that 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p act as agonists of NIB1 in promoting phase separation.

We further monitored NIB1–YFP condensation in N. benthamiana leaves upon treatment with nucleotide analogues. Consistent with findings from MST (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g), 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP and 2′3′-cGAMP did not trigger condensate formation, whereas 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP induced far fewer condensates than 2′,3′-cAMP (Extended Data Fig. 6g,h). Co-incubation with NVR1, rice plant RNA (OsRNA) and 2′,3′-cAMP resulted in larger NIB1–YFP droplets in vitro, which required the NVR1 catalytic activity, NIB1 binding sites and 2′,3′-cAMP to achieve optimal effect (Extended Data Fig. 6i). In vitro reconstitutions revealed that NIB1–YFP formed droplets, dependent on 2′,3′-cAMP, OsRNA and salt, as well as protein and macromolecular crowding agent concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 6j–m).

To investigate the biochemical consequences of NIB1 liquid–liquid phase separation, we examined its effect on NVR1 enzymatic activity. NVR1 was more active in the presence of NIB1, and the substrate degradation increased with higher concentrations of NIB1 (Fig. 3a). When the C-terminal IDR-containing fragment was deleted (NIB1(ΔIDR)), the influence of NIB1 on NVR1 activity was reduced or negligible (Fig. 3b), suggesting that the IDR steers NIB1 to boost the NVR1 enzymatic activity. Consistently, the NVR1–NIB1 complex synthesized a higher amount of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than NVR1 alone, which also required the IDR in NIB1 for increased activity (Fig. 3c). Similarly, when co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves, full-length NIB1 significantly enhanced NVR1 in generating 2′,3′-cNMP compared with NIB1(ΔIDR) (Extended Data Fig. 6n). We subsequently evaluated the effect of NIB1 on NVR1-induced cell death in N. benthamiana and found that removing the IDR from NIB1 largely abrogated its potentiation of NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). Additionally, the NIB1(R49A) and NIB1(G50A) mutants also showed compromised acceleration of NVR1 catalysis (Fig. 3d) and the NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6q,r). In sum, catalytically active NVR1 stimulates NIB1 phase separation, which in turn enhances NVR1 activity in degrading RNA and synthesizing 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, thereby inducing plant cell death through a positive feedback loop. In this mutual potentiation interaction, NIB1 uses both the IDR and the RNA-binding sites in the RRM to amplify and transduce NVR1-generated signalling molecules.

Right, reaction completion after 25 min, calculated as (intensity of hydrolysed RNA)/(intensity of undigested RNA) × 100%. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. b, Left, NIB1 (1 μM), but not NIB1(ΔIDR), stimulated NVR1 activity in a 25-min assay. Right, quantification of band intensity. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. c, 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p produced by NVR1 (1 μM) after co-incubation with NIB1 or NIB1(ΔIDR) (1 μM) for 25 min. d, NIB1(R49A), NIB1(G50A) and NIB1(4A) (1 μM) activity in promoting the production of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p is compromised by NVR1 (1 μM), assayed for 25 min using rRNA as substrate (2 μg in 20 μl). In a–d, data are mean ± s.d. of n = 3 biologically independent replicates. Statistical differences were determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test.

NIB1 is highly expressed in multiple rice tissues (Extended Data Fig. 7a). To investigate the NIB1 function in plant defence, we used CRISPR–Cas9 to generate NIB1-knockout (NIB1-KO) and NIB1-overexpression (NIB1-OE) rice lines (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). NIB1-OE and NVR1-OE plants showed similar transcriptional changes, with 553 (59%) of the upregulated genes overlapping (Fig. 4b), including genes associated with response to biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence (Fig. 4c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 were downregulated in NIB1-KO plants but markedly upregulated in NIB1-OE plants (Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with the RNA-seq data and the levels of defence hormones salicylic acid and jasmonic acid (Fig. 4d). C. medinalis larvae gained more weight after feeding on the NIB1-KO lines than with the wild-type plants; by contrast, their growth was retarded on the NIB1-OE plants (Fig. 4e). Females and larvae preferred NIB1-KO over wild-type and NIB1-OE plants in oviposition and feeding-choice assays (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Insect feeding strongly induced MYC2 in wild-type rice, but the induction was much weaker in the NIB1-KO mutant (Fig. 4f). NIB1-OE plants had reduced tillering, partly resembling the NVR1-OE phenotype (Extended Data Fig. 2l), whereas NIB1-KO plants grew well and produced more tillers (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7h), probably reflecting their differences in immune intensity. These results suggest that NIB1 positively regulates plant defence responses.

a, Representative plants of ZH11, NIB1-KO and NIB1-OE lines. b, Venn diagram showing overlap of genes that are upregulated in NVR1-OE and NIB1-OE rice leaves. WT, wild type. c, Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the upregulated genes common to NIB1-OE and NVR1-OE rice. P < 0.05. d, Jasmonic acid (JA) and salicylic acid (SA) contents in ZH11, NIB1-KO and NIB1-OE leaves, detected using HPLC. e, Weights (right) of C. medinalis third-instar larvae fed on the 12-day old rice plants for 3 days (left). f, MYC2 expression increased markedly in ZH11 leaves but weakly in NIB1-KO leaves during feeding by C. medinalis third-instar larvae. g, NVR1 (1 μM) treatment triggered a lower-intensity ROS burst in NIB1-KO rice leaves in 30-min assays, compared with wild-type ZH11 leaves. h, Right, NVR1-induced cell death was compromised in NbGRP7-KO leaves (3 dpi). Right, colour-coded stacked bars display the percentages of each cell death score (0–5; n = 11 leaves). i, Jasmonic acid and salicylic acid contents in ZH11, NIB1-KO and NIB1-KO leaves expressing NIB1, NIB1R49A or NIB1G50A in 12-day old rice plants. j, 2′,3′-cNMP binding mutations impaired NIB1-mediated resistance to insect feeding. Twelve-day-old rice plants were inoculated with C. medinalis third-instar larvae for three days. k, Overexpression of NIB1(ΔIDR) did not restore the compromised insect resistance in NIB1-KO plants. Third-instar larvae were weighed after placing on the rice plants for three days. Data are mean ± s.d. Sample sizes: n = 3 biologically independent samples (d,i); n = 12 (e) and n = 19 (j) larvae; n = 6 (g). Statistical differences were determined by two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test (g), one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s (d,e,i,j) or Dunnett’s (k) multiple-comparisons test.

We next investigated whether the NVR1-induced plant defence responses were contingent on the presence of NIB1. Treatment of rice plants with purified NVR1 induced ROS production, which was attenuated in NIB1-KO lines (Fig. 4g). Consistently, NVR1-induced cell death was mitigated in NbGRP7-KO leaves compared with wild-type N. benthamiana (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 7i,j). Thus, the RNA-binding protein NIB1 mediates NVR1-dependent induction of plant defence response.

To further determine whether NIB1 senses 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p to mediate NVR1-induced immune activation, we generated overexpression complementation lines in NIB1-KO rice plants, including wild-type NIB1, NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A. The two recognition-deficient complementation lines were unable to rescue the immune responses in NIB1-KO mutants, as indicated by defence hormone accumulation (Fig. 4i), insect resistance (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b) and the expression of MYC2, COI1 and NPR1 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Expression of NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A in wild-type rice plants did not lead to a clear upregulation of these defence genes (Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Together, these results show that NIB1 activates plant defence against insect feeding and that sensing of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p is crucial for this immune function of NIB1.

MST assays with NIB1(ΔIDR) exhibited similar binding affinity to 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P as wild-type NIB1 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 8f). However, overexpression of NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP in NIB1-KO rice plants did not rescue the compromised insect resistance (Fig. 4k). Moreover, treatment with 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP induced condensate formation in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/NIB1-KO plants but not in 35S::NIB1ΔIDR-YFP/NIB1-KO plants (Extended Data Fig. 8g,h). Thus, both ligand recognition via RRM and subsequent phase separation via IDR are essential for the NIB1-dependent defence response.

To connect the NVR1–NIB1 module to the plant defence network, we performed IP–MS on leaves co-expressing NIB1–YFP and NVR1. EDS1, CDPK and MAPK6 were identified as NIB1 interactors (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Comparison with the NVR1 interactome revealed that the shared components were enriched in herbivore-response pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9b).

EDS1 is a central immune signalling node35,36,37. In SLC assays, NIB1 interacted with rice EDS1 (Extended Data Fig. 9c). EDS1–YFP co-immunoprecipitated with NIB1–Flag in N. benthamiana (Fig. 5a), and His–NIB1 pulled down EDS1–Flag from N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assays showed that NIB1 interacted with EDS1 in the nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 9e), and the NIB1–EDS1 interaction was enhanced by NVR1 via its RNase activity (Fig. 5b). Catalytically active NVR1, but not the inactive NVR1(H-doub) mutant, stimulated NIB1 recruitment of EDS1 into sparkly nuclear condensates (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9f). We then used EDS1–NES–mCherry to test whether EDS1 acts as a nuclear carrier for NIB1. When EDS1–NES–mCherry was largely retained in the cytosol, NIB1 continued to form nuclear condensates in the presence of NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 9g), indicating that NIB1 nuclear condensation is independent of EDS1 and supporting the role of NIB1 as a scaffold for EDS1 recruitment.
