Middle, number of condensates per nucleus. Right, NIB1 and EDS1 partition coefficients with empty vector, NVR1 or NVR1(H-doub). mCh, mCherry. d, Salicylic acid and jasmonic acid contents in ZH11 and eds1 leaves. e, MYC2 expression in CR-eds1 leaves with or without 6 h of C. medinalis feeding (ZH11 set to 1). f, Decreased resistance in eds1 plants, evaluated by C. medinalis larvae weight after 3 days of feeding. g, RT–qPCR of PR1 and MYC2 in ZH11 leaves, NIB1-OE ZH11 leaves and NIB1-OE CR-eds1 leaves. h, PR1 and MYC2 expression in wild-type, NIB1-KO and CR-eds1 leaves 6 h after treatment with water, 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP, ApG>p or 8-Br-AMP (50 μM each). i, NbPR1 and NbMYC2 expression in wild-type, NbGRP7 and epss leaves 6 h after treatment with water or 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP. j,k, Spraying 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP enhanced plant insect resistance in the laboratory (j) and the paddy field (k), as indicated by growth of C. medinalis third-instar larvae fed with water- or 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP-treated ZH11 plants. l, A proposed model of GRP in the plant defence response to insect oral secretory RNaseT2. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 biologically independent samples (d,e,g–i); n = 6 (b) or 8 (c, middle) nuclei; n = 20 condensates (c, right); n = 11 (f) or 12 (j,k) larvae. Results in a represent three independent experiments; experiments in j,k were repeated twice. Statistical differences were analysed by two-tailed t-test (d–f,j,k); one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (b,c,g); or two-way ANOVA with the two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli (h,i). Scale bars, 10 μm (b) and 5 μm (c).

The rice CR-eds1 mutant generated by CRISPR–Cas9 accumulated lower levels of jasmonic acid and salicylic acid (Fig. 5d) and expressed lower levels of COI1, NPR1 and ERF1 (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j). The induction of MYC2 expression in response to insect feeding was minimal in the rice CR-eds1 mutant (Fig. 5e). CR-eds1 plants were more vulnerable to C. medinalis (Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 9k,l), demonstrating a vital role of rice EDS1 in insect resistance.

The immune activation phenotype of NIB1 overexpression was highly attenuated in the rice eds1-KO mutant and NIB1-triggered induction of defence genes PR1, MYC2, COI1, NPR1 and ERF1 was diminished in CR-eds1 rice plants (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 9m,n). Treatment with 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p induced the expression of PR1 and MYC2 in rice leaves, but this induction was compromised in NIB1-KO and CR-eds1 plants (Fig. 5h). Similarly, 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP treatment upregulated NbPR1 and NbMYC2 expression in wild-type N. benthamiana but not in NbGRP7-KO or N. benthamiana epss (eds1a, pad4, sag101a, sag101b) mutants (Fig. 5i). RNA-seq analyses of N. benthamiana wild-type, NbGRP7-KO and N. benthamiana epss leaves treated with 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP showed that the differential gene expression observed in wild-type N. benthamiana was largely absent in NbGRP7-KO and N. benthamiana epss mutants (Extended Data Fig. 9o,p). The upregulated genes were predominantly enriched in defence pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9q). These data demonstrate that EDS1 and NIB1 are important signalling components for the immune function of 2′,3′-cAMP.

Herbivore-induced endogenous 2′,3′-cAMP concentration reached around 21 μM in rice (Fig. 1g), comparable to the 50 μM concentration used in our assays. Treating N. benthamiana leaves with 21 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h upregulated NbPR1 and NbMYC2 to similar levels as the 50 µM 2′,3′-cAMP treatment. Thus, the herbivore-induced endogenous accumulation of 2′,3′-cAMP is physiologically sufficient to elicit defence responses (Extended Data Fig. 9r). Exogenous application of 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP via spray significantly enhanced plant resistance against herbivory under both laboratory and paddy field conditions (Fig. 5j,k and Extended Data Fig. 9s).

Given that plant TIR proteins function as 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP synthases3, we tested whether the TIR-induced immunity also involves NIB1 or the orthologous GRP by expressing the TIR domain of Arabidopsis RPS4 (RPS4TIR) in NbGRP7-KO lines. Arabidopsis RPS4TIR-induced cell death in NbGRP7-KO leaves showed slight attenuation at 36 h post-infiltration (hpi) but became obvious and complete by 56 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10a–c). The cell death triggered by the rice TIR-only protein OsTIR was also slightly attenuated in the NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO mutants when observed at 40 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10d–g), with obvious cell death and completion at 68 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10h). These results suggested a general role of GRP in sensing the 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated mono- and dinucleotides. In sum, our results show that GRPs sense the nuclease products of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, contributing to the activation of the EDS1-dependent signalling pathway (Fig. 5l).

Plants express many cell-surface and intracellular immune receptors to perceive alien molecules and activate defence38,39. Here we found that the rice GRP NIB1 interacts with invading RNaseT2 and senses 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p to induce plant defence. The presence of NVR1 orthologues in oral secretions of the piercing-sucking pest Apolygus lucorum (ALR1; data not shown) and chewing insect C. medinalis suggests that T2-family ribonuclease effectors are conserved across divergent feeding types and may be a broadly deployed strategy in plant–insect interactions. Given the involvement of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP in abiotic stresses40,41,42,43, it is worth further investigating the role of GRPs in leveraging biotic and abiotic stresses. Whether and how plants discriminate between different sources of second messengers are also important questions to address.

Condensates or membraneless compartments are engaged in a variety of plant developmental and stress response processes44,45,46,47. NIB1, as a sensor, perceives 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p and forms nuclear condensates that recruit the core immune regulator EDS135,36,37 and activate downstream signalling pathways, highlighting protein phase separation as a mechanism in response to second messengers. Our study focuses on the immune function of nuclear NIB1, whereas the biological roles of its cytoplasmic condensates deserve future investigation. Exogenous spraying of these RNA degradation-derived signalling molecules triggered plant defence responses, highlighting their application potential as immune activators. Our study opens a door for exploring the engagement of RNase products in plant defence, adaptation and development.

Plant TIR-catalysed and NAD+-derived products induces formation of EDS1–SAG101–NRG1 and EDS1–PAD4–ADR1 heterotrimers, as well as oligomerization of ADR1 and NRG1 as calcium channels at the plasma membrane, to confer immunity. The link between TIR nuclease-derived 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and EDS1 remains unclear, and the nuclear function of EDS1 in TIR-mediated immunity is unknown. Our unpublished data show that 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP does not contribute to the EDS1–SAG101–NRG1 or EDS1–PAD4–ADR1 heterotrimer formation, consistent with the proposed role of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP in amplifying rather than initiating TIR signalling3. In bacteria, 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP have been shown to modulate activities of transcription factors48. 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP-induced NIB1 condensate in the nucleus recruits EDS1 to trigger defence, potentially via transcriptional modulation, providing a possible explanation for the biological relevance of plant TIR nuclease activity. Plant TIR-only proteins but not TIR–NLR receptors possess nuclease activity—thus, TIR nuclease activity and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP are likely to be involved in TIR-only-mediated basal immunity but not TIR–NLR-mediated effector-triggered immunity3,49, consistent with the weak contribution of GRPs towards TIR-induced cell death phenotypes in N. benthamiana. The T2 RNase NVR1 produces ApG>p, and the nuclease product spectrum of plant TIR-only proteins awaits further studies. Future studies could investigate whether other GRPs are also involved in perceiving such nuclease products and their interactions. Detailed analyses of NIB1 condensate components will add valuable knowledge to understanding this nuclease-based defence pathway.

Phytophagous insects, especially mesophyll feeders, generate various small molecules from biopolymers by injecting digestive enzymes into plant tissues, in addition to mechanical injury. Detection of DAMPs is essential for plants to activate defence programmes. Although the wide-scale cultivation of transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis insecticidal proteins has effectively controlled the lepidopteran chewing insects in the field, heteropteran mesophyll feeders such as the mirid bug A. lucorum (Miridae) and the green stink bug N. viridula (Pentatomidae), are less sensitive to these proteins and are emerging as a threat to agriculture50. Our findings show that plant GRP is a sensor of the invading RNase products and orchestrates immune responses to activate an EDS1-dependent signalling pathway, providing a potential target for advanced plant protection technologies.

Rice plants (Oryza sativa L. subsp. japonica cv. ZH11) grown in experimental fields in Shanghai or Hainan, or under controlled greenhouse conditions, were used for stable transformation and CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene knockout. To generate overexpression lines, the cDNAs of NVR1 and NIB1 (transcript ID: Os03t0670700-04) were introduced into the pCAMBIA1300 vector under the control of the CaMV 35S promoter, or as indicated. DNA sequences were analysed using SnapGene 6.0.2. Following transformation, more than ten independent overexpression lines were obtained for both NVR1 and NIB1. The NIB1-KO rice mutants, as well as N. benthamiana NbGRP7-KO plants, were generated by WIMI Biotechnology. NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO lines were generated by Wuhan BioRun Biosciences. For transient expression assays, leaves from 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants grown in a greenhouse at 22 °C under long-day conditions (16 h light:8 h dark) with a photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) of 112.81 μmol m−2 s−1.

N. viridula was collected from the Hangzhou farm, Zhejiang Academy of Agricultural Sciences, and reared on kidney beans and corn in a growth chamber at ~28 °C. C. medinalis was at first collected from the experimental farm in Songjiang, Shanghai, China in 2022. To maintain genetic homogeneity and sensitivity, the insects were continuously laboratory-reared for more than 15 generations without pesticide exposure. Larvae were reared on fresh wheat seedlings, and adults were supplied with a 15% honey solution. The colony was maintained under strictly controlled conditions at 26 °C with 12 h light:12 h dark photoperiod.

N. viridula saliva was collected using a Parafilm sachet feeding assay. Following a 24-h starvation period, 20 adult N. viridula were supplied with 1 ml of 2.5% sucrose solution encapsulated within Parafilm membranes. After 24 h of feeding, the saliva-containing sucrose solution was collected and concentrated using Amicon Ultra-0.5 centrifugal filter devices (Millipore). Salivary proteins were mixed with 4× SDS loading buffer, denatured at 95 °C for 10 min, and separated by SDS–PAGE. The salivary proteome was subsequently analysed via LC–MS/MS (Novogene) (Supplementary Table 1).

The constructed vectors were introduced into A. tumefaciens strain GV3101 (pSoup-p19). After cultivation in medium at 30 °C overnight, the bacteria were collected and resuspended in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM MES, 150 μM acetosyringone, pH 5.8), and incubated at room temperature for 2–3 h. The bacterial suspensions were adjusted to OD600 = 0.6 and infiltrated to the leaves of 4-week N. benthamiana with needleless syringe. For co-expression, equal volumes of Agrobacterium suspensions (adjusted to an OD600 of 1.0) carrying the respective constructs were mixed for co-infiltration.

The protein coding sequences for His- and GST-tagged proteins were cloned into pColdTF/pET-28a and pGEX-4T vectors, respectively, and expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) pLysS cells. Cultures were grown in LB medium at 37 °C to OD600 of 0.5, followed by induction with 0.5 mM IPTG at 15 °C for 16 h. Cells were collected, lysed by sonification in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, pH 8.0) and centrifuged at 20,000g for 30 min at 4 °C. For His-tagged proteins, the supernatant was loaded onto Ni-NTA resin, washed with a wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, pH 8.0), and subsequently eluted with an elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). For the purification of GST-tagged proteins, the supernatant was incubated with Glutathione Sepharose 4B resin, washed with lysis buffer (140 mM NaCl, 27 mM KCl, 10 mM Na2HPO4, 1.8 mM KH2PO4), and eluted with the same buffer supplemented with 10 mM reduced glutathione. To obtain nucleic acid-free NIB1–YFP, recombinant protein-expressing E. coli cells were collected and resuspended in cold TBS (20 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.6) at 9 ml per gram of wet cells. TieChui E. coli Lysis Buffer (ACE Biotechnology) was added at one-ninth of the suspension volume, followed by incubation at 4 °C for 10 min to lyse the cells and digest bacterial DNA and RNA. After centrifugation at 20,000g at 4 °C, the clarified supernatant was subjected to affinity purification.

To investigate potential protein–protein interactions, coding sequences were cloned into JW772-35S-cLUC or JW771-35S-nLUC. The constructs were introduced into Agrobacterium GV3101 (pSoup-p19), and the bacterial cultures were co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves as described above. After 48 h of transformation, fluorescence was detected and imaged using the Tanon Chemi Dog 5200T Imaging System to visualize protein interactions.

The interacting protein candidates were co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves for 48 h. The leaves were collected, homogenized in liquid nitrogen and suspended in IP lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 20% glycerol, 0.5% NP-40, 1×protease inhibitor cocktail). The mixture was centrifuged at 14,000g for 10 min. The supernatant was incubated with GFP magnetic beads for 2 h at 4 °C and then washed 5 times in IP lysis buffer. Beads were boiled at 95 °C in 50 μl 4× SDS loading buffer for 10 min and analysed by immunoblotting. Measurements were repeatedly taken from separate lysates to confirm repeatability.

For immunoblotting, proteins were separated by 4–20% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. After blocking with 5% (w/v) non-fat milk, the membranes were incubated with the following primary antibodies: mouse anti-DDK (Flag) monoclonal antibody (ZSGB-BIO, TA-05, clone OTI11C3, lot no. 230021225; 1:2,000), mouse anti-His monoclonal antibody (OriGene, TA150088, clone OTI2B5; 1:5,000), mouse anti-plant actin monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AC009, clone AMC0496, lot no. 9100009001; 1:5,000), horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated rabbit anti-Myc-tag monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AE102, clone ARC5004-12-HRP, lot no. 3523030201; 1:5,000), rabbit anti-GFP-tag polyclonal antibody (ABclonal, AE011, clone N/A, lot no. 3560104011, RRID: AB_2771922; 1:2,000), rabbit anti-β-actin monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AC026, clone ARC5115-01; 1:10,000), rabbit anti-histone H3 monoclonal antibody (HUABIO, ET1701-64, clone JJ090-07, lot no. H641565025; 1:5,000), rabbit anti-PEPC polyclonal antibody (Agrisera, AS09 458, lot no. 2410; 1:2,000), or a custom rabbit anti-NVR1 polyclonal antibody generated for this study by ABclonal Technology (1:500). For unconjugated primary antibodies, the membranes were subsequently incubated, as appropriate, with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (ZSGB-BIO, ZB-2305, lot no. 219760308; 1:10,000) or HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) (ZSGB-BIO, ZB-2301, lot no. 242521208; 1:10,000). Chemiluminescent signals were detected using ECL reagents and imaged with a Tanon 5200T Imaging System.

The YFP-tagged protein was immunoprecipitated using GFP magnetic beads at 4 °C for 2 h. After washing the beads 5 times with IP lysis buffer, the bead-bound proteins were treated with 10 mM TCEP and 50 mM CAA (in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate) at 95 °C for 10 min.

Samples were prepared via a filter-aided sample preparation method using Vivacon 500 filters (10,000 MWCO; Sartorius), sequentially washed with 8 M urea and 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and digested overnight with 1 μg of trypsin (Promega). Following desalting with Pierce C18 Spin Tips (Thermo Fisher Scientific), peptides were dried by centrifugation at 10 °C, reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid, and subjected to LC–MS/MS analysis.

LC–MS/MS analysis was performed using a timsTOF Pro 2 mass spectrometer coupled to a nanoElute liquid chromatography system (Bruker Daltonics). In brief, 200 ng of peptides were separated on a reversed-phase analytical column (25 cm × 75 µm internal diameter, IonOpticks) over a 60-min gradient at a flow rate of 300 nl min−1 and a column temperature of 50 °C. The mobile phases consisted of buffer A (0.1% formic acid in water) and buffer B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile). The gradient elution profile was set as follows: an increase to 22% buffer B from 0 to 45 min, up to 37% buffer B from 45 to 50 min, and a final step at 80% buffer B from 50 to 60 min. The mass spectrometer was operated in DDA-PASEF mode with the following parameters: capillary voltage, 1,500 V; dry gas flow, 3.0 l min−1; and drying temperature, 180 °C. The collision energy was linearly ramped as a function of ion mobility.

The raw LC–MS/MS data were searched against the N. benthamiana protein sequence database (Nbe_v1.1_pep.fa.gz), downloaded from NbenBase (https://nbenthamiana.jp/downloads), using MSFragger within FragPipe v22.0. Trypsin was specified as the digestion enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages. Precursor and fragment ion mass tolerances were set to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine (+57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification, whereas methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da) was included as a variable modification. Peptide and protein identifications were filtered to a 1% false discovery rate using a target-decoy strategy (Supplementary Tables 3, 6 and 7).

His–TF and His–TF–NIB1 were incubated with 15 μl of Ni-NTA resin for 1 h at 4 °C. Protein extracts from leaves expressing EDS1–Flag were added to each resin and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The resin was washed 6 times with IP lysis buffer, resuspended in 50 μl of 4× SDS loading buffer and heated at 95 °C for 10 min. Bound proteins were analysed by immunoblotting.

Target coding sequences were cloned into pCAMBIA1300S-cYFP or pCAMBIA1300S-nYFP. Following co-expression of the fusion proteins in N. benthamiana leaves for 2 days, YFP signals were acquired by 20× water immersion objective through Leica TCS SP8 STED 3X.

MST was used to determine the protein–protein interactions and the binding affinities of NIB1 and its mutated versions to the indicated small molecules or RNA, protein labelling was performed in strict accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, the purified recombinant proteins (NIB1–GST, NIB1(R49A)–GST, NIB1(G50A)–GST and NIB1(4A)–GST) at a concentration of 10 μM were labelled with NT–647–NHS using the Monolith Protein Labeling Kit RED-NHS 2nd Generation (NanoTemper Technologies). The labelled NIB1–GST and its mutants were adjusted to 50 nM in PBST buffer (PBS, with 0.05% Tween-20) and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p (5 μM to 0.000153 μM) were added separately. For characterizing the interaction between NVR1 and NIB1 (NIB1RRM and NIB1GRR), 10 μM NVR1–TF was labelled and adjusted to 40 nM in PBST buffer. Subsequently, NIB1–GST, NIB1RRM–GST and NIB1GRR–GST (2.5 μM to 0.0000763 μM) were added separately. For protein–RNA interaction, the Cy5-labelled FLS2 3′-UTR served as the target and adjusted to 20 nM. NIB1–GST and the mutant fusions (10 μM to 0.000306 μM) were incubated with target. To access the interaction between NIB1(ΔIDR) and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P, the labelled NIB1(ΔIDR) was used as target and adjusted to 50 nM. The target protein was independently mixed with 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P (10 μM to 0.000306 μM). Furthermore, to test the binding affinity of NIB1–GST with 3′,5′-cAMP, 3′,5′-cGMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP, GMP and the unrelated cyclic dinucleotides 2′,3′-cGAMP, 50 nM labelled NIB1–GST was used as target and independently mixed with the indicated compounds (15 μM to 0.000458 μM). A Microscale Thermophoresis Monolith NT.115 instrument (NanoTemper Technologies). was used to measure binding reactions at 25 °C, 40% MST power and 20% LED power. Measurements were repeatedly taken repeatedly from separate protein preparations to confirm repeatability. The curve was fitted using the MO.AffinityAnalysis_x86_2.3.0.7385, and the dissociation constant (Kd) value was determined.

NIB1–YFP fusion protein and its various mutants were purified by Ni-NTA resin. NIB1–YFP droplets with 10% PEG 8000, or as specifically indicated, were observed by Leica TSC SP8 STED 3× 100× oil immersion objective. The droplets were bleached by 100% intensity 488 nm laser and the recovery was recorded every 3 s 290 ms for 50 frames in FRAP. Fusion of NIB1 droplets was recorded through time-lapse photography. Droplet diameters were measured from microscopy images using Fiji (ImageJ, version 1.54f).

Target proteins fused with fluorescent protein (YFP or mCherry) were co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves. Condensates in leaves were observed by Leica TSC SP8 STED 3X (Leica) 40 × oil immersion objective. To prevent fluorescence bleed-through during imaging, all images were acquired using the sequential scanning mode on a Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope. YFP was excited with a 488 nm laser and detected at 498–540 nm, and mCherry was independently excited with a 561 nm laser and detected at 600–630 nm. The images of condensates were analysed using Fiji (ImageJ, version 1.54f). Line profile analysis was performed to evaluate co-localization of the proteins. To quantify the partition coefficient of the EDS1–mCherry into NIB1–YFP condensates with or without NVR1, regions of interest of equivalent size were analysed. The partition coefficient (Kp) was defined as the ratio of intracondensate EDS1 fluorescence intensity to that of the extracondensate background.

The Cy5-labelled AttRNAser (83 nt) used as substrate for NVR1 digestion was obtained through in vitro transcription using T7 RiboMAX Express RNAi System. A reaction mixture containing 0.5 mM Cy5-UTP and 1 mM synthesized AttRNAser DNA template (sequence listed in Supplementary Table 13) were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. The template DNAs were then removed by 0.5 μl RNase-Free DNase (Promega) at 37 °C for 30 min. In the RNase activity assay, 2 μM Cy5-AttRNAser was incubated with 0.02 μM NVR1 in buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 5 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP, 0.5 μl RNase Inhibitor at 25 °C for 20 min. The reaction was stopped by 400 μl stop solution (40 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 500 mM NaCl). Then RNAs were purified with PCIA solution (phenol:chloroform:isopentyl alcohol, 25:24:1) and the RNA pellet was resuspended in 1× TBE urea loading buffer. The RNA was then separated using 16% urea polyacrylamide gels at 150 V for 90 min and subsequently detected with a Amersham Typhoon 5.

Cy5-labelled FLS2 3′-UTR were synthesized in vitro using the HyperScribe T7 High Yield Cy5 RNA Labeling Kit (APExBIO) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, the 3′-UTR sequence of FLS2, as previously described44, was amplified using a forward primer containing a T7 promoter sequence (TAATACGACTCACTATAGGGGAAGTTTAGCAGCAAAGC) and a reverse primer (GTTCATCAAAACCAAATTTC). One microgram of DNA template containing a T7 promoter was combined in a 20 μl reaction volume. The reaction mixture consisted of 2 μl of 10× Reaction Buffer, 2 μl of T7 RNA Polymerase Mix, 2 mM each of ATP, GTP, and CTP, 1.5 mM UTP and 0.5 mM Cy5-UTP. The reaction was thoroughly mixed and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. Following transcription, the DNA template was digested by adding 1 μl of DNase I and incubating at 37 °C for 15 min. The synthesized Cy5-labelled RNA was subsequently purified via phenol/chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation. To evaluate the labelling efficiency, the absorbance of the purified RNA was measured at 260 nm and the Cy5 maximum excitation wavelength using NanoDrop.

Cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions were extracted according to the manufacturer’s manual instructions of Minute Cytoplasmic and Nuclear Extraction Kit for Cells. In brief, leaves (0.1 g, co-expressing NIB1–YFP and EDS1–mCherry with or without NVR1 for 48 h) were homogenized in cytoplasmic extraction buffer. Following centrifugation (14,000g, 5 min, 4 °C), the cytoplasmic supernatant was collected. The pellet was lysed in nuclear extraction buffer through repeated cycle of vortexing and ice incubation, and then centrifuged through a pre-chilled filter cartridge (14,000g, 30 s) to collect the nuclear extract. Histone H3 and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) served as nuclear and cytoplasmic markers, respectively, to confirm successful fractionation.

Leaves were incubated in DAB solution (1 mg ml−1 DAB, 0.05% Tween-20, 10 mM Na2HPO4, pH 5.8) for 4–5 h in the dark. Bleaching buffer (ethanol:acetate:glycerol, 3:1:1) was added to displace DAB stain, and the sample was heated to 90–95 °C 3–5 times until the chlorophyll was removed completely. The samples were immersed in 50% glycerol for imaging.

RNaseT2 proteins were filtrated from the genomes of plants (Gossypium hirsutum, Nicotiana tobacum, O. sativa), fungi (Fusarium graminearum, M. oryzae), insects (N. viridula, A. lucorum, Nilaparvata lugens, Aphis gossypii, C. medinalis, H. armigera) and mammals (Homo sapiens and Rattus norvegicus) using PF00445 HMM search or NCBI blastp. The GRPs (GRPIVa) encoded in genomes of 18 plant species of 14 families (Physcomitrella patens, Adiantum capillus, Cycas revoluta, Picea abies, Nymphaea colorata, O. sativa, Zea mays, Sorghum bicolor, Brachypodium distachyon, G. hirsutum, Arabidopsis thaliana, Vitis vinifera, Carica papaya, Cucumis sativus, Glycine max, Solanum lycopersicum, Solanum tuberosum and Populus trichocarpa) were filtrated under the condition of only one PF00076 domain. The genomes were obtained from Phytozome (https://phytozome-next.jgi.doe.gov/) or NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/), and insect proteomes were obtained from the NCBI Protein database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/). All filtrated proteins in these two classes were aligned by MUSCLE 5.1, trimmed using trimAl 1.2. The phylogenetic tree was constructed by using IQ-TREE 2.2.0 and annotated by Evolview v3. Conservation diagram of amino acid residues was shown using Jalview 2.11.2.5.

Total RNA was extracted from leaves of ~4-week-old wild-type O. sativa ZH11 and transgenic lines, as indicated. Leaves of four-week-old tobacco (N. benthamiana) were infiltrated with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h, followed by RNA extraction. RNA-seq was performed by Personalbio. Clean reads were aligned to the O. sativa reference genome (GCF_001433935.1_IRGSP-1.0_genomic.fna; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_001433935.1/) or the N. benthamiana reference genome (Niben.genome.v1.0.1; https://solgenomics.net/ftp/genomes/Nicotiana_benthamiana/assemblies/) using HISAT2. Differential gene expression analysis was subsequently performed using DESeq, with differentially expressed genes identified based on the thresholds of |log2(fold change)| > 1 and P < 0.05. GO enrichment and volcano plots were generated using R v4.3.2 in RStudio 2023.09.1. The differentially expressed genes and corresponding GO enrichment results are provided in Supplementary Tables 2, 4, 5, 8–12.

The third-instar C. medinalis larvae were placed on leaves of the 12-day-old rice seedlings of the indicated lines. Larval weight was recorded after the feeding for three days. Oviposition selection assay was conducted in nylon mesh cages (90 × 70 × 90 cm). Three one-month-old, uniform rice plants per genotype were grouped and arranged triangularly to prevent positional bias. 15 pairs of newly emerged moths were mated for 48 h. Subsequently, males were removed, and the 15 mated females were released into the cage centre with a 15% honey solution. After 24 h of oviposition at 26 °C (12 h:12 h light:dark photoperiod), the total number of eggs laid on the three plants of each genotype was summed. The assay was repeated with three independent cages. Oviposition preference was quantified by the oviposition index: OI = (T − C)/(T + C), where T and C are the number of eggs in the mutants and wild type, respectively. The deviation of the oviposition index against 0 was tested using a one-sample Student’s t-test.

For larval feeding preference, leaf segments (3 cm) from 3 plant lines were arranged equidistantly in a circle within a Petri dish. Ten third-instar larvae (pre-starved for 2 h) were introduced to the centre. After 1 h of selection in darkness, the number of larvae settled on each plant was recorded. The selection rate was calculated as Ntarget/Ntotal selection × 100%, where Ntarget and Ntotal selection represent the number of larvae on a specific plant and the total number of larvae making a definitive choice, respectively.

For field test, wild-type ZH11 seeds were sown in soil, and 35-day-old plants were transplanted into six 1 m × 1 m field plots. Each plot was surrounded by two rows of rice plants serving as buffer rows, and all six plots were maintained within mesh enclosure. Four weeks after transplantation, the plots were arranged in an alternating pattern and sprayed with either water or 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP. Following treatment, 20 mated female C. medinalis moths were released at the centre of the enclosure. Once rolled-leaf shelters became visible, the number of shelters was counted. Insects and plant positions were randomized in laboratory assays, field treatments followed an alternating design, and outcomes were assessed blind to genotype or treatment.

Leaves tissue of 4-week-old rice plants were ground into powder with liquid nitrogen and resuspended in 500 μl ethyl acetate. Following vortex for 1 min and centrifugation at 14,000g for 10 min at 4°C, the supernatant was transferred and dried in vacuum concentrator and resuspended in 30 μl 30% (v/v) methanol. The samples were centrifuged at 14,000g for 15 min and the supernatant was applied to the LC–MS/MS on a QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX) for analysis. Salicylic acid samples were diluted to 1/100 with 30% (v/v) methanol.

Leaf sheath segments of 2 mm were excised from 2-week-old rice seedlings and pre-incubated overnight in sterile distilled water. The samples were then treated with water or purified recombinant His–NVR1 protein in buffer containing 20 μM luminol and 10 μg ml−1 HRP. Luminescence was recorded at 1-min intervals for 100 min with Varioskan Flash multireader (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

NVR1 (1 μM) and the rRNA substrate (2 μg) were incubated in a 20-μl reaction mixture at 25 °C for 25 min. The reaction was stopped by adding methanol, and the mixture was centrifuged at 12,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected and analysed by liquid chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC–HRMS) using a Q Exactive quadrupole-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometer coupled to a Dionex Ultimate 3000 RSLC (HPG) ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography system. The injection volume was 1 μl. The samples were separated on an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column with a particle size of 1.8 μm. The mobile phase were water (A) and methanol (B), each containing ammonium formate (2 mM). The gradient elution was set as follows: 0–6.5 min, 2% methanol; 6.5–8.5 min, 20% methanol; 8.5–11 min, 98% methanol; 11.1–15.0 min, 2% methanol. The flow rate was consistently set to 0.40 ml min−1, and the column temperature was precisely maintained at 40 °C. Detection was performed in positive-ion mode using a heated electrospray ionization source. LC–HRMS data were analysed using Thermo Scientific Xcalibur 4.1.50.

Extraction of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP was performed as described3. Leaf tissue was ground into powder with liquid nitrogen. Samples were resuspended in 600 μl 4% acetate containing 1 mM IBMX and vortexed for 2 min. The supernatant was extracted twice with 800 μl chloroform. The samples were dried through vacuum spinning and resuspended in 50 μl sterile water.

The dissolved samples were subjected to analysis by LC–MS/MS on a QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX) coupled to an Agilent 1290 LC system. Chromatographic separation was achieved using a Waters XSelect HSS T3 column with a particle size of 2.5 μm and dimensions of 100 mm × 3.0 mm. Sample of 1 μl was injected. The mobile phase consisted of water (A) and methanol (B), both containing 2 mM ammonium formate. The gradient elution method was used as follows: 0–2.5 min, 2% B; 2.5–3.0 min, 2–70% B; 3.0–5.0 min, 70–99% B; 5.0–7.0 min, 99% B; 7.1–10 min, 2% B. The flow rate was set at 0.4 ml min−1, and the column temperature was maintained at 40 °C. Metabolites were detected using electrospray ionization in negative ion mode with multiple reaction monitoring. The mass spectrometer parameters were as follows: −4,500 V of capillary voltage, 500 °C of source temperature, 50 psi of ion source gas 1 (GS1) and gas 2 (GS2), and 35 psi of curtain gas. Data acquisition and analysis were performed using Analyst 1.6.3 software (AB SCIEX).

Step 1. To a stirred solution of 2′,3′-O-isopropylideneguanosine (1.0 eq) in anhydrous tetrahydrofuran (THF) at 0 °C under an inert atmosphere, trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) (1.0 eq) was introduced, followed by the dropwise addition of pyridine (2.5 eq). The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 2 h. Next, isobutyryl chloride (1.0 eq) was added dropwise at 0–5 °C, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature for an additional 1 h. After quenching and extraction, the crude product was obtained and purified by C18 flash chromatography. The final product was characterized by LC–MS and 1H NMR spectroscopy for structural confirmation. Step 2. To a stirred solution of the Step 1 product (1.0 eq) and starting compound 2 (1.0 eq, CAS: 104992-55-4) in dichloromethane (DCM) at 0 °C, 5-(benzylthio)-1H-tetrazole (5-BTT) (1.0 eq) was added. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 3 h. Reaction solution washed water and brine, the DCM solution was concentrated under vacuum, the crude by C18 flash purification. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 3. To a stirred solution of iodine (1.0 eq) in a THF:water:pyridine mixture (10:5:1, v/v/v), the Step 2 product was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 1 h, followed by the addition of 10% sodium sulfite solution until the colour disappeared. The reaction mixture was then concentrated under vacuum, and the residue was extracted with ethyl acetate. The organic layer was dried over anhydrous Na2SO4, filtered, and concentrated under vacuum. The crude product was used directly in the next step without further purification. Confirmed by LC–MS and 31P NMR. Step 4. To a stirred solution of the Step 3 product (1.0 eq) in DCM, trifluoroacetic acid was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at 45 °C for 4 h. After completion, the solution was concentrated under vacuum. Due to the product’s high water solubility, the residue was purified directly by C18 flash chromatography. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 5. To a stirred solution of the Step 4 product (1.0 eq) in acetonitrile, N-methylmorpholine (1.0 eq), 2-methoxy-1-ethanesulfonyl chloride (2.0 eq), trimetaphosphate tri-tetrabutylammonium salt (1.0 eq), 1H-4(5)-nitroimidazole (0.1 eq), and DBU (3.0 eq) were added sequentially under nitrogen protection. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature until completion. MgCl2 (2.0 eq) was then added, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature. After completion, the solvent was concentrated under vacuum, and water was added to the residue to adjust the pH to 3–4. The mixture was extracted with ethyl acetate, washed, dried, and concentrated to obtain the crude product, which was further purified by preparative HPLC and lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 6. To a stirred solution of the Step 5 product (1.0 e) in THF, HF (6.0 eq) was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at 50 °C until completion. Triethylamine was then added to the residue to adjust the pH to 6–7, and the mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure to obtain the crude product. The crude product was purified by preparative HPLC and lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 7. To a stirred solution of the Step 6 product (1.0 eq) in methanol (10 volumes), NH3/methanol (10.0 eq) was added at 0 °C. The reaction mixture was stirred at 0 °C for 6 h until completion. The methanol solution was then concentrated under vacuum and the residue was purified by preparative HPLC followed by lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR.

NIB1–GST was incubated with 10 μl of glutathione agarose resin at 4 °C for 2 h. Empty vector (encoding TF tag) or NVR1 products were added to the resin for an overnight incubation at 4 °C. Then the resin was treated with 100 μl of 80% acetonitrile and 5% formic acid and incubated at 25 °C for 30 min before proceeding with liquid chromatography analysis.

The 12-day-old rice seedlings were sprayed with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP, 8-Br-2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p for 6 h, with water and 8-Br-AMP as controls. After treatment, RNA was extracted, and the expression levels of defence genes were analysed by RT–qPCR. Leaves of 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants were infiltrated with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h, and gene expression was analysed by RT–qPCR.

AlphaFold2 was used to predict the structure of the NVR1–NIB1 complex. The 3D structures of 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP were obtained from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), and ApG>p was modelled using ChemBioDraw Ultra 14.0. The ligands were optimized using density functional theory (DFT) in Gaussian 16 and prepared for docking with NIB1 using AutoDockTools 1.5.7. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock 4.2.6 with ligand-specific grid boxes at a spacing of 0.375 Å. Grid dimensions were adjusted to 46 × 50 × 50 for 2′,3′-cAMP, 50 × 56 × 56 for 2′,3′-cGMP and 100 × 100 × 100 for ApG>p. The Lamarckian genetic algorithm was applied with 50 runs, a population size of 150 and 2.5 × 106 energy evaluations. The lowest-energy poses were analysed using PyMOL 2.5.5 and LigPlot+ 2.2.8.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software). Comparisons between two groups were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. For comparisons among multiple groups, one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s or Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test was used, as appropriate. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test or the two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli was performed, as indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05, with a false discovery rate of 5% for analyses using the Benjamini–Krieger–Yekutieli procedure. For violin plots, width indicates data density, lines show the median and quartiles, and dots represent individual values. Details of the statistical tests are provided in the corresponding figure legends.

Sequences used for phylogenetic analyses were obtained from Phytozome (https://phytozome-next.jgi.doe.gov/), NCBI Datasets (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/) and NCBI Protein database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/). #1286. Inter relief at Thuram injury, but muscular issues becoming a problem

There is mixed news from the Inter medical staff, as while Marcus Thuram’s injury is not as serious as first feared, he is out of international duty along with Ange-Yoan Bonny and Aleksandar Stankovic.

The injuries have been piling up for the Nerazzurri and they are beginning to affect their international careers as well.

Thuram withdrew from the France squad for the Nations League matches against Italy and Belgium due to a hamstring issue.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport and Sky Sport Italia, tests showed this is just a fatigue problem and there are no lesions, so Thuram hopes to be available when Serie A returns and Inter face Atalanta on November 22.

However, this is just the latest setback after Bonny pulled out for the Ivory Coast and Stankovic was forced to abandon the Serbia national team.

Lautaro Martinez, Luis Henrique, Benjamin Pavard, Curtis Jones and John Stones have been out for a while already leading up to this break, while Djed Spence is out of England’s Nations League fixture with Croatia tomorrow.

By calculating all the players in the squad, they have missed 15 of the first 37 competitive matches for Inter this season.

#1285. The unexpected email that led to Bukayo Saka's Socrates Award win at the Ballon d'Or: Inside Arsenal star's secret humanitarian work after his surprise win at London ceremony

Published: 08:07 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 08:13 EST, 11 November 2026

The sight of Bukayo Saka hobbling down the red carpet at the Ballon d'Or ceremony came as a surprise. Only those closest to him knew why he was there, and the years of toil that led to this moment.

While his England team-mate Harry Kane claimed the night's top on-pitch prize, Saka – who had suffered a thigh injury just days before against Kane's Bayern Munich – was at the London Palladium to collect the Socrates Award for his humanitarian work.

Joining a roll of honour that includes previous winners Vinicius Junior, Sadio Mane and Luis Enrique, Saka walked onto the stage, reached into his suit pocket and read a letter from a 14-year-old boy in Rwanda whose eyesight had been restored through his charity work.

Now, Daily Mail Sport can reveal the scale of the Arsenal star's involvement over the last four years with the BigShoe charity, which funds operations, feeds children and helps with disaster relief across the world. From restoring the eyesight of that 14-year-old in Rwanda to helping provide life-saving procedures for 120 children in Nigeria, Saka's impact goes far beyond the stadiums he dazzles in.

And this is no passive act of philanthropy. BigShoe president Valerie Fiesser's phone is often inundated with messages from Saka when the charity is delivering projects in poverty-stricken countries such as Nigeria and Rwanda. Many of the project ideas come from the 25-year-old himself.

'Bukayo is really, really productive,' Fiesser tells Daily Mail Sport. 'He is really pushing how he wants to help. I think for him it is never fast enough to help. Sometimes Bukayo comes up with projects and he says, "Shouldn't we help here?" So he is really interested in it. It is not like he is just sending money and saying, "OK, nice, we'll do a project in Nigeria".

Bukayo Saka was handed the Ballon d'Or Socrates Award for his humanitarian work last month

Saka has worked with BigShoe charity for years - helping those in poverty-stricken countries

In 2023, Saka donated 50 containers to help provide shelter for 255 people impacted by the devastating earthquake in Morocco

'When we are on the ground, he is texting, "Is everything alright? Is everybody safe? Are all the children safe? Which services do we have? Can I see pictures? Send me pictures, send me pictures, send me pictures!"

BigShoe, a German-based charity founded during the 2006 World Cup, began years ago by funding life-changing surgery for Nourisson, a young girl from Togo born with a cleft lip and palate. The Togo national team, playing at their first World Cup, were based in the city of Wangen im Allgau, which brought the story to prominence in Germany.

The charity is now a worldwide network of football stars, fans and partners, with more than 10,000 children around the globe having benefitted via projects ranging from medical supplies to shelter and food. The organisation has also worked with Antonio Rudiger, Paul Pogba and Saka's ex-Arsenal team-mates Mesut Ozil and Oleksandr Zinchenko.

Fiesser vividly remembers how Saka first got in touch, in early 2022.

'He just really randomly wrote us an email,' she says. 'He asked us if we can help together in Nigeria after seeing a project of another soccer player. He said, "I want to help children, I want to help people and can we do something". (It was) really just random.'

That initial conversation quickly developed into a project in late 2022 which funded 120 life-changing medical operations for children in Nigeria. Some of the youngsters were suffering from brain tumours, while others required treatment for hernias.

'This was an incredible project because it was the first project in Nigeria together with him,' she says. 'It was really life-changing for the children because some had a brain tumour, some had hernia problems.'

Saka has since helped support healthcare check-ups for more than 580 children in Rwanda and provide disaster relief after devastating earthquakes in Morocco and Turkey, while his involvement has extended far beyond financial backing.

The charity is now a worldwide network of football stars, fans and partners, with more than 10,000 kids having benefitted via projects ranging from medical supplies to shelter and food

'We did a disaster relief where we provided homes for the earthquake victims in Morocco and Turkey and he was asking questions like, "Do they have electricity there?"' she says.

'He is really thinking, "Is it worth it, does it make sense to do this, or is it just putting the container and then the people do not have water and they cannot live there?" So he is really, really smart. And yes, I think he is an amazing human.

'It was never about him. It was always about the children and how we can help. It was never like, "OK, we are talking to one of the best players of the world." I think he is raised like this. His family made him the man he is now.

'I think he is raised like this, that you have to be a good human being and to help others and just have an impact in life.'

Saka and his family are directly involved in the projects, identifying communities in need and deciding exactly how support should be delivered. His mother, Adenike, is a key figure.

'We decide together where we can help, how we can help and then we actually help together,' Fiesser says. 'Me and his mother WhatsApp, call regularly. She has played a big part and is a driving force.

'Three months ago we renovated a school in Rwanda and we provided them with water filters for clean drinking water. We also built girls' changing rooms, a new soccer pitch and a new library. Bukayo's family was on the ground, twice.

'We decided after we saw that the families are really hungry in this area to do food packages. It is our next project in November and December.

'He (Saka) really wants to make a difference. He wants to change lives.'

While Saka will continue to chase trophies in Arsenal red and England white, his greatest legacy may ultimately be measured in the lives he has changed far beyond the football pitch.

#1284. Manna: ‘Napoli will be ready in January, did not spend wisely last season’

Napoli director Giovanni Manna assures they have ‘clear ideas’ on how to improve Max Allegri’s squad in January, but admits ‘perhaps we didn’t spend our money wisely’ last season.

The Partenopei are struggling badly both in Serie A and the Champions League, with calls for the coach to be sacked, perhaps rescued only by the injury crisis decimating his team.

President Aurelio De Laurentiis seems determined to stick with Allegri and that means giving him more alternatives in the January transfer window.

“We have clear ideas on how to improve, correct and complete the squad, and we will ensure that we are ready in January,” director of sport Manna told Radio Kiss Kiss.

It is very likely that several players will be moved on, above all Lorenzo Lucca and Noa Lang, who have failed to live up to expectations following big money moves.

“Last season we spent a lot, but perhaps we didn’t spend our money wisely, and I say that being fully aware of the criticism I deserve for that. The President and I never held back when it came to investments, but we did have to respect certain financial parameters, so over the summer opted for more of an austerity approach.

“Nobody banned us from making moves, but some situations were stalled and that blocked others in the transfer market. We’ll be ready in January.”

Manna was slightly reassured by the 1-1 draw with Lazio that saw Napoli go into the break for international duty.

“I saw an encouraging reaction in the second half, showing the kind of energy required to get out of the current situation, so we are hopeful things will be better once we get a few players recovered from injury.

“We are well aware of the situation, and we are not happy with how the season has started. Aside from injuries, if we did something wrong or made incorrect evaluations, we are here to work and fix it.

“It’s important to find a sense of calm and not try to experience every game as if it’s the last, as that doesn’t help.”

There have been reports that Napoli are pursuing Torino winger Alessio Cacciamani, who had already been targeted by Roma over the summer.

“He is certainly an interesting prospect who impressed at Juve Stabia and is showing his potential, but that’s a long way from saying he’ll come to Napoli,” replied Manna.

“There are many players we are keeping an eye on, and he is one of the most interesting young Italian players right now.”

Monza centre-forward Gustavo Varela is another name mentioned with regards to a potential January swoop from Napoli.

“He is a good player, but right now we have Lucca, who is young and can cover that role. Then we’ll see, based on who leaves, what will happen. He is certainly doing well, but I doubt Monza will want to sell a player like that in January, seeing as they are fighting for their Serie A safety.

“Napoli have not made any steps for Varela so far, we’ve done nothing.”

#1282. How Michael Carrick's Man United fell apart: Players' bust-up on flight back from Madrid, weakness in training and on touchline - and why dressing-room sources believe divided board 'hung him out to dry'

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 10:30 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 10:42 EST, 11 November 2026

For the last two days, Michael Carrick has followed his familiar route towards Manchester United’s training base, nudging his black Land Rover past the security barrier at Carrington before 8am, and making his way into work just as he has for much of the last two decades as a player, coach and head coach at the club.

While Carrick's fate has been decided by men in suits in Monaco and Manchester, he has put on his training gear and gone through the motions of coaching whichever players are left during the international break.

It has become increasingly apparent that Carrick was a dead man walking in the two weeks since the United board gave him a stay of execution and bought themselves time after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last month.

Having effectively been brought in as a caretaker when United plucked him off the beach in Barbados in mid-January, he left much the same way: merely keeping the seat warm for Mauricio Pochettino in the chaotic days that have led to his sacking.

Sources close to the United dressing room believe Carrick has been ‘hung out to dry’ as United dithered over his future and then began a futile attempt to appoint Pochettino as his replacement in secret.

This is the story of how Carrick's United fell apart. It is the story of how disgruntled players aired their dirty laundry in public and clashed in private. It is the story of how the club's boardroom became the backdrop for an executive power struggle. And it is the story of how the magic touch that saw Carrick land the job permanently just five months ago deserted him...

Michael Carrick is out as Manchester United manager - just ten league games after guiding United to third and being handed a two-year contract

Carrick has had to turn up as normal at Carrington this week even as the world knew he was for the chop. Some dressing-room sources say he has been 'hung out to dry'

Carrick would have seen the writing on the wall when he got up to give an impressive speech at a dinner in the Heritage Suite at Old Trafford on Friday night to celebrate the 40th anniversary of Sir Alex Ferguson’s appointment.

The significance of the occasion was not lost on Carrick. Ferguson was brought in to succeed Ron Atkinson on the same date in November 1986 with United one place above the relegation zone. Having boxed himself into an identical corner, Carrick too was on borrowed time.

Two days later, he stood helplessly on the touchline at Old Trafford as United played out a ridiculous 4-4 draw with Aston Villa. Twice his team fought back from two goals down, but it was the final proof for United bosses that change was unavoidable.

The biggest club in English football having to endure the humiliation of at least two weeks in the relegation zone was too much for them to stomach.

His body language after the Bournemouth game when a tearful and crestfallen Carrick offered what looked like a farewell wave to the Stretford End – four days after he approached fans in Como to apologise for an equally painful 4-1 Champions League surrender – suggested he was already done.

The 45-year-old limped on to another defeat at Chelsea, then presided over a barmy 3-2 comeback win over Roma and the bonkers draw with Villa. A consummate and composed midfielder for United, Carrick of all people knew this wasn’t the way football should be played.

All the while, he spoke like a man who could turn things around. They always do. But the performances and results told a different story.

His critics would argue that someone whose only previous job in management was at Middlesbrough should never have been put in charge of United in the first place.

Others would say the bravest move by the club would have been to thank Carrick for his admirable efforts in securing third place and Champions League qualification last season, and move on in the summer when Pochettino would have been available for free before signing a new contract as US coach with a £7million release clause.

Matheus Cunha's late winner sealed a remarkable comeback win over Roma last week - but it promised to be a false dawn for Carrick

The 45-year-old's body language after an earlier loss to Bournemouth had suggested he was done back then, with Carrick appearing to wave farewell to the Stretford End

Instead, Carrick was rewarded with a two-year deal in May and the wheels fell off in spectacular fashion. Rather like his friend and former team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, the honeymoon period gave way to something altogether less appealing.

At least Solskjaer stuck around for three more years. Having beaten the Norwegian to the job in January, Carrick’s reign lasted less than 10 months.

The similarities between the two men are striking. Ex-players who basked in the glory days under Ferguson and know what it takes to succeed at Old Trafford, but were incapable of lifting the modern-day Manchester United to similar heights.

Having replaced Ruben Amorim and inspired a remarkable turnaround in the second half of last season, Carrick must have thought he had a chance.

His calm demeanour and experience of life in the Old Trafford pressure cooker that had played a part in his appointment was in contrast to the emotional incontinence of Amorim. How strange then that it has given way to such calamity and chaos.

United got off to the worst possible start by losing at newly-promoted Hull City in August. Tigers boss Sergej Jakirovic belittled them by saying his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis might as well have been sipping a cup of tea, and the hits have just kept on coming for Carrick.

Aside from Bournemouth, there were the late equalisers scored by Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Dominic Solanke for Everton and Tottenham, the controversial winner conceded to 10-man Manchester City, crashing out of the Carabao Cup to Brighton after giving up a two-goal lead, and the defeats in Europe by Atletico Madrid and Como after going behind in the opening seconds.

By the time Alysson scored in the first minute for Villa on Sunday, United’s defence had become as leaky as the Old Trafford roof. The four goals Carrick’s side conceded took it to 15 in his final four games.

United's defence has been leaky all season long, with Ainsley Maitland-Niles' stoppage-time equaliser at Hill Dickinson Stadium among the goals to cost them valuable points

By the time Alysson scored in the first minute for Aston Villa on Sunday, United’s defence had become as leaky as the Old Trafford roof. They let in 15 in his final four games

So why the alarming decline from last season? The United players haven’t looked sharp after a disjointed World Cup summer that involved a more relaxed one-week training camp in Ireland. There have been too many injuries.

Some players have spoken of a drop-off in training under Carrick and his backroom staff. Others feel that the switch to a more possession-based 4-2-4 system was asking too much of a group who aren’t suited to it.

There was surprise that a man so invested in the club's academy used so few young players. Harry Amass was left kicking his heels despite the chronic shortage of left backs, JJ Gabriel's shock exit was an unwelcome distraction, and Shea Lacey's re-emergence came too late.

It would be grossly unfair to pin this all on Carrick though. He is just the latest unfortunate to pay the price for the shambles at United which runs from the boardroom to the dressing room.

Amid ongoing uncertainty over his future, there has been a power struggle behind the scenes between director of football Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell over who to replace him, while sources close to the Glazer family have revealed a growing dissatisfaction at how minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos are running the club.

United failed Carrick in the transfer market last summer with a futile pursuit of his No 1 midfield target Elliot Anderson, and instead delivered Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.

Carrick could see trouble on the horizon when he spoke to the media at Carton House in Maynooth during that pre-season camp in early August, but tried not to rock the boat.

It was the day his daughter Louise was getting her A-level results. ‘You know, we would like more, we need to keep pushing for more,’ he said, using the word ‘push’ another nine times.

There has been a power struggle behind the scenes between director of football Jason Wilcox (centre) and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell (left) over who to replace Carrick

Some players have spoken of a drop-off in training under Carrick and his backroom staff

Carlos Baleba followed but an ankle injury meant that he couldn’t play until October, and the £70m signing then suffered a hamstring injury.

United blundered catastrophically by focusing on midfield and delaying improvements to other areas of the team until next summer. In particular, the decision not to sign cover for Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko backfired spectacularly as both players succumbed to injury.

Lisandro Martinez called out United’s underwhelming recruitment in Madrid by saying he expected more of Wilcox, and he isn’t the only one who feels that way.

Tielemans gave a terse ‘no comment’ when he was asked on camera about his team-mate’s remarks, but it’s understood the two players clashed on the team flight back to Manchester as cracks began to show in an increasingly unhappy camp.

The camaraderie fostered by rounds of golf involving Carrick and the players during the break in Ireland was beginning to fall apart.

It came to a head when captain Bruno Fernandes became the second member of the leadership group to speak out of turn, questioning Carrick’s tactics after the loss to Como.

Having continuously defended his players in the face of criticism from some of his former United team-mates over their lack of effort, Carrick’s spiky response that ‘if you don't run forward and you don't run back, you aren’t going to win’ perhaps revealed his true feelings about this group.

He and Fernandes settled their differences in a clear-the-air meeting, but the questions didn’t go away. When he was asked about their relationship again at the end of what proved to be his final pre-match press conference last Friday, Carrick tapped his inquisitor on the shoulder as he left the room at Carrington and said with a smile: ‘Nice try!’

It was typical of Carrick, who often met questions with the knowing grin of a man who couldn’t say what he really thought.

Lisandro Martinez and Youri Tielemans clashed on United's flight back to Manchester following the former's incendiary comments after a loss to Atletico Madrid

One issue has been Carrick’s rather passionless appearance on the touchline. ‘He doesn't upset anyone, but doesn't inspire anyone either,’ remarked one dressing room source

It got to the point where he was encouraged by the club to be a little more forthcoming in press conferences. There have been some barbed post-match exchanges in TV interviews with Sky Sports and Viaplay this season, and the five-minute monologue before the Bournemouth game was pure theatre.

But on the whole, Carrick’s ability to play a straight bat in front of the cameras was a welcome change for the Old Trafford hierarchy compared to the loose-lipped Amorim – particularly with the Amazon Prime documentary-makers following their every move.

‘He talks a lot but doesn't say much,’ said Roy Keane, never Carrick’s biggest fan, on Sunday. ‘I don't know if that's a tactic, like a politician.’

More of an issue was Carrick’s rather passionless appearance on the touchline, which seemed to be reflected in his team at times.

Always dressed in black, a hand placed studiously on his chin, it has contrasted with more animated adversaries such as Unai Emery, Roberto De Zerbi and Diego Simeone in recent weeks.

‘He doesn't upset anyone, but doesn't inspire anyone either,’ remarked one dressing room source.

The fans were always behind him though, even the ones who may have accepted some time ago that a change was needed. Support and sympathy were never in short supply for a coach who has been let down by the men in the directors’ box and the players on the pitch.

That much has been abundantly clear by the abuse meted out to Ratcliffe and Co this season, and the unprecedented scenes when the fans turned on the players after Bournemouth.

Carrick looks set to be replaced by former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino (right)

Carrick has been known to stand alongside them in the past, and it would be no surprise to see him there again in future.

‘Oh, it’s Carrick you know…’ echoed his tribute song from the Stretford End as he disappeared down the tunnel for the last time on Sunday evening.

So another bites the dust. A good man. A United man. The right man for the job? Maybe not, as it turns out. That poisoned chalice now passes to Mauricio Pochettino.

#1281. Official: Mbappé out of Italy vs. France, as Zidane warns ‘we won’t risk him’

France coach Zinedine Zidane confirms Kylian Mbappé is out of tomorrow’s Nations League match against Italy. ‘He is injured, so we will not risk him.’

It kicks off at San Siro on Thursday at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

Les Bleus are top of the Nations League group with 10 points, followed by Italy on seven and Belgium six, so the two spots going into the quarter-finals are all to play for.

There had been reports in L’Equipe that Mbappé had skipped training today with a hamstring issue and was therefore a major doubt to feature in this Matchday 5 fixture.

When Zidane arrived for his press conference this evening, he spoke to RAI Sport and confessed the decision had already been made.

“No, Mbappé will not be there tomorrow,” said the coach and former Juventus midfielder.

“He is injured, so we will not risk him. We’ll see if he can recover in time for the next game.”

France will face rock bottom Turkiye in the final Nations League fixture on Sunday evening, while Italy go head-to-head with Belgium in Brussels.

Les Bleus are already missing Marcus Thuram, Pierre Kalulu, Aurelien Tchaouameni, Manu Koné, William Saliba, Jules Koundé, Maxence Lacroix, Ousmane Dembélé, Maghnes Akliouche and Esteban Lepaul.

Italy should field youthful players to conquer France and leave out veterans

I do not expect Italy to defeat France, more likely a 2-2 draw…

It’s the Belgium match which will decide the fate of the Gli Azzurri, and I have full confidence that we will win that game either 3-2 or 2-1.

Odegaard with a poor pass in the middle of the park, but Konsa produced a tremendous block to stop Kane’s left-footed shot across Raya.

The corner is flicked to the back post, where Calafiori was inches away from scoring from six inches out. Close to Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

The game is stretched now and quite entertaining, a very different feel to Arsenal’s Premier League assignments. Konsa realised Arsenal were short of numbers and lunged in against Harry Kane, hacking him down at the expense of a booking. Rice and his team-mates recovered well against the counter in any case.

Kane with another superb pass, perfectly curled around Timber into the path of Alphonso Davies who finishes beyond Raya. Kane had too much space in the middle of the pitch, Madueke perhaps guilty of not narrowing in.

Kane has played some absolutely absurd passes in this first half and that was the best yet. Alphonso Davies is so quick that Arsenal were never going to catch him, and the pass was so good that David Raya could not come to it.

Harry Kane with an OUTRAGEOUS assist, and Alphonso Davies equalises 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/6cGXrUloHW

A word of warning for Arsenal is that Kompany has Lennart Karl and Luis Diaz sat on his bench. At least one of those attackers will be on at half-time unless something changes.

Arsenal winning most of the aerial battles and duels for second balls at the moment, Bayern not building any pressure or fluency. There has been the odd flash of danger when Kane flips a pass in behind but Arteta’s team are comfortable at the moment.

Odegaard almost finds Eze with a lovely disguised through ball.

There was a 30-second flurry from kick-off where Bayern had Arsenal’s penalty area under siege, but Arsenal have controlled the game well since and they have another corner. Odegaard has enjoyed the extra space on offer all game. Arsenal’s captain whips the corner to the back post where Guimaraes was free, but he shins a volley wide.

That makes two goals in three games for Eze. Although he got hooked at half-time in one of them (against Forest on Sunday). It feels like that’s probably how it’s always going to be with a player like him, to be honest. Highs and lows.

Arsenal had to wait for the VAR intervention, but they have the lead in the Allianz thanks to a high-quality goal. Odegaard released Eze in behind with a lovely ball forward, and the former Palace man steadied himself before drilling a left-footed shot across Neuer.

VAR has given it, and Eze strikes Arsenal into the lead at the Allianz 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/i1LjrZVnbI

Good work from Odgegaard in midfield, one lovely flick to help Arsenal restore some control.

Then Eze puts the ball in the net with a fine finish across Neuer but the flag goes up for offside. This will be checked by VAR... Stanisic, the Bayern left-back, was lingering behind his team-mates on the opposite side of the pitch.

Kane’s range of passing in evidence again, with a driven diagonal over Gabriel’s head towards Saibari but he could not control the ball that was fizzed towards him. Kane is drifting towards the left to open up the pitch for those crossfield passes.

Arsenal caught out on the break by Harry Kane taking a goal kick, from which he picked out Davies with a raking pass down the left. Saibari helped the ball on for Gnabry who was free on the right, but Raya was down quickly to save and Rice cleared.

Arsenal have a corner, after a nice Madueke backheel released Timber. They have the upper hand in this game, but they have lost a major attacking reference with Saka going off. It’s a case of Arsenal’s weakest area being weakened further. From the corner, Calafiori stretches out a leg but directs the ball over.

Arsenal enjoying the lion’s share of possession so far, which is perhaps a reflection of Bayern’s absentees. Kane has just dropped into his own box to receive a pass, and Konsa followed him all the way.

Alphonso Davies runs beyond the Arsenal defence for the first time in the game after Gnabry dribbles past Madueke, but Gabriel made a good challenge from the wrong side.

Ezri Konsa just followed Harry Kane all the way into the Bayern penalty area. Kane loves to drop deep and Arsenal have clearly decided to stick on him, no matter where he goes. For a few moments, Kane was the deepest Bayern player and Konsa was the most advanced Arsenal player.

Havertz has been booked for a foul on Stanisic. Bayern have not been able to build a head of steam as an attacking force so far, but their pressing has forced Arsenal into longer balls forward. No serious chance so far.

So it is now Madueke on the right and Eze on the left for Arsenal. A shame for the spectacle that neither Saka nor Olise are on the pitch, and the Arsenal man had started the game quite brightly.

Saka had a quick chat with Arteta before going down the tunnel. He gestured towards his left quad.

Big problem here for Arsenal: Bukayo Saka has collapsed to the turf after playing a pass, and he looks to have pulled a muscle in his thigh. That is surely his race run tonight, and it looks like he could be out for a few months based on how he went down. Eze is coming on.

The Arsenal fans high up in the Allianz Arena are singing Saka's name as he hobbles off the pitch. He looks very, very uncomfortable. Eze is coming on, so Madueke will move to the right.

Saibari with a cheap loss of possession in midfield, allowing Saka to go straight at the heart of the Bayern defence. He feeds Havertz on the right, but from the German’s cross the ball would not quite drop for Timber or Saka in a crowded box. There looks space on offer for Arsenal. Do they have the speed and quality to exploit it?

Arsenal’s first foray into the attacking third comes from a Raya clip to Timber, pushed well on from right-back, and the defender’s header inside to Saka was a clever one. Madueke received the next pass, but his touch was a little heavy.

Kim players a good switch of play to Laimer, but Calafiori and Rice snuff out any danger and Guimaraes does well to win a midfield foul.

Calafiori was super advanced within the first 30 seconds, straight into an attacking midfield zone. Davies is indeed playing as a left-winger for Bayern in front of Stanisic. In the very early exchanges, Bayern are enjoying more of the ball, but the game still to settle into a pattern.

Arsenal get the game under way, playing in their navy away kit.

The rain continues to lash down. Jurgen Klopp, Germany’s manager, is in the stands having a flim-flam with Rafael Benitez, who has dashed to Bavaria from Anfield where he watched Liverpool vs Villarreal last night.

It seems like Vincent Kompany may have taken a leaf out of Thomas Tuchel’s tactical book. When Arsenal came here in 2024, Tuchel deployed two left-backs on that flank (Mazraoui and Guerreiro) after saying in the press conference that Arsenal’s right-sided attackers were the danger. Kompany appears to have done the same here with Davies, usually a left-back, starting as a winger.

We are going to have to play I expect three or four different games at different stages throughout the game, so we need to have everybody ready to adapt throughout.

Kane has already played against Arsenal since leaving Spurs, so some of the vinegar has gone out of that sub-plot but it is still worth noting that he has scored 15 goals in 22 appearances against them. Several of those goals have been penalties, but Kane is so much more than a goalscorer these days, especially at Bayern where at times he appears to have a free role.

A fascinating aspect of tonight’s game is how Konsa and Gabriel decide to deal with him. Will Arsenal commit to a man-to-man press, with the centre-backs following Kane well beyond the halfway line, or preserve a more zonal approach?

Manchester United are now 4-0 down against a Como team managed by Cesc Fabregas. There is still 15 minutes or more to play. You can follow the rest of the game here to see if they can stem the bleeding.

Will the substitutes again make the difference for Arsenal tonight? In each of their last three league victories, they have won because of goals scored by substitutes. This speaks to the quality of Arteta’s squad, obviously, but also to the Arsenal manager’s ability to pick the right players for the right moments. Over the last year or so, this has become a real strength.

Karl had been expected to replace Olise on the right, but Kompany looks to have stiffened up his midfield by starting Pavlovic, Laimer and Bischof. It will be interesting to see how Saibari and Kane dovetail, two stick-on strikers. It is not Bayern’s strongest team, with Luis Diaz also on the bench.

Bayern Munich starting XI: Neuer, Stanisic, Kim Minjae, Upamecano, Davies, Pavlovic, Laimer, Bischof, Gnabry, Saibari, Kane

Subs: UIreich, Urbig, Ito, Tah, Brown, Luis Diaz, Boey, Sapoko Ndiaye, Karl, Binder

There was little doubt that Arteta would view this game as one that suits Jurrien Timber rather than Ben White. Arsenal’s manager has changed tack by starting Calafiori, who was rested for Arsenal’s first two Champions League games, but Bayern at the Allianz is a significant step up in grade. Madueke rewarded for his showing at Forest.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard; Saka, Havertz, Madueke

Subs: Kepa, Meslier, White, Mosquera, Lewis-Skelly, Zubimendi Merino, Eze, Gyokeres, Dowman

🔵 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🟡 Two changes for tonight's test ✊

Vincent Kompany is in the building. It wasn’t clear whether the Bayern head coach would be able to attend tonight’s game because he’s been battling a nasty virus over the last few days. He did not do the usual pre-match press conference yesterday but clearly feels well enough to be here tonight.

In an extract from Sam Dean’s new book on Arsenal’s resurgence under the Spaniard, he reveals that Mike Ashley was keen to bring Arteta to Newcastle United in 2019.

Sam writes: “Arteta also did not have a coaching staff assembled. It is believed that he tried to bring some key individuals on board, such was his interest in accepting Newcastle’s offer, but that the timing was not right for the people he truly wanted. In the end, much to the frustration of Newcastle and Ashley, he said no.”

Arsenal: The Inside Story of Arsenal’s Rebirth Under Mikel Arteta (Pan Macmillan, RRP £22).

This is a proper heavyweight clash but, sadly for the neutrals watching, Bayern are missing some big players. Michael Olise is suspended, Jamal Musiala is injured and Joshua Kimmich is unavailable following the death of his father.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Arsenal won 3-1 at the Emirates in November in a performance of real class. It was arguably their most complete showing of the entire campaign.

Ice cold from Martinelli 🥶 https://t.co/uQEHb4x7eH

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.
