#1240. Most expensive goal in Liverpool history gives Iraola era lift-off

A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

Anfield has witnessed plenty of significant goals down the years but never had this crowd seen one that cost £248m to make. Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an important afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

But Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

“I’m very happy,” Iraola said. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”

And how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

With the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

"He's GOT to hit the target!" Yasin Ayari missed a golden chance to put Brighton ahead against Liverpool 🫣 https://t.co/Qz7G3sXCpP

Liverpool’s lead was secured with an element of good fortune but, equally, the tenacity of Ronald Araújo and Wirtz was instrumental in pressing Brighton back to the point that they were panicking; Wirtz’s shot, deflected off Pascal Gross past Bart Verbruggen, compounded it all.

“I think everyone in the stadium – and you as well – felt there was a missed opportunity for us,” groaned Fabian Hürzeler, the visitors’ head coach. “It’s not only after the goal or the goals they scored. Before they scored, we had two big chances. I think it was just the difference that they scored and we didn’t score.”

It would be wrong to say Wirtz was doing cartwheels – perhaps he knew immediately he would not get the goal – but it was an important moment for him and you could feel the sense of goodwill towards him from team-mates and supporters alike.

Florian Wirtz's deflected shot has put Liverpool ahead minutes after Brighton had a great chance of their own ⚽️ https://t.co/b6mRvl2rSR

Remarkably, this was the first time Liverpool had scored in the first half at Anfield in a Premier League fixture since May 9 and, with that momentum, it led to one of those periods when they started attacking in waves and carried the crowd with them.

What they needed was a second goal to arrive quite quickly and that is what happened when Barcola won possession, scuttled forward and played a perfectly weighted bobbling ball into Isak’s path; the Swede did the rest, calmly finishing from eight yards.

Everything with Isak feels to be going under the radar at the moment, but that is six goals in six Premier League appearances. He is starting to show the consistency and killer instinct that everyone felt he would. Iraola will be hoping it continues for the foreseeable future.

Alexander Isak scores to double Liverpool's lead at Anfield! 💥 https://t.co/oYs2jnHZEb

“The performance was really good,” said Isak, the quiet assassin. “We were really solid against a really good team. The first half is what we really want to be about. It was about intensity, winning balls and countering.”

Brighton, as much as Hürzeler protested, could not properly recover, though this is no criticism. They remain committed to attack, they struck the frame of the goal when Ayari tried to punish an Alisson Becker mistake and the desire to keep pushing ensured Liverpool could never relax.

What Liverpool had going for them this time, however, was an intensity to preserve a clean sheet and nobody embodied the indefatigability more than Araújo, the Uruguay international whose loan from Barcelona is looking an increasingly shrewd piece of business.

Two moments stood out: one thunderous tackle on substitute Malick Yalcouyé in front of the Main Stand that had the locals roaring their approval, another in the first half when he was on the floor but still managed to head away to thwart Maxim De Cuyper.

They remember those moments as much as the stardust that Barcola and Isak provide. Put it all together and it might just be a launchpad for Iraola.

"The performance was really solid" Alexander Isak reacts after scoring in Liverpool's win against Brighton 🗣️ https://t.co/Zei2tmWVix

Iraola has his first Premier League home win in charge of Liverpool thanks to a 2-0 victory over Brighton. The hosts netted twice in the first half through Wirtz’s deflected strike off Gross and Isak’s close-range finish. This result moves Liverpool above Chelsea and up to fourth, just a point behind third-place Brighton, who suffer their first defeat in any competition since August 30.

Three points at Anfield 😍 #LIVBHA https://t.co/AnAlNgOzlu

Still, Brighton can’t find a way through Liverpool’s resilient defence. Araujo’s well-time sliding challenge on Kostoulas draws huge cheers from the home fans.

Ronald Araujo has become a cult figure very quickly and he’s just provided the moment of the second half with a challenge that was a well received by those in the Main Stand as a goal. Liverpool are working relentlessly to preserve their clean sheet and Andoni Iraola is imploring his players to retain their focus until the end.

There will be four minutes of added time. Brighton need a goal as soon as possible. Liverpool are closing in on an impressive win.

So wasteful from Brighton... They have a great chance to put the ball into the box with a free kick, but De Cuyper wastefully launches it out of play. With Gross also stood over it, you expected him take it. Liverpool then make a late change as Tsimikas replaces Kerkez for the final few minutes.

Gakpo drives forward and smashes a wild long-range shot wide. His end-product has been lacking today, but he’s undoubtedly caused Brighton problems with his dribbling, movement and directness.

A spell of Brighton pressure ends as Rutter can’t quite find Kostoulas with a low cross. The young striker stays down and replays show that Jacquet stood on his foot as the defender attempted a clearance. However, it’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR. There wasn’t much in the challenge at all.

Kerkez scampers into Brighton’s box, reaching the byline, but he can’t dig out a cross as the chance disappears. Brighton will need to throw everything forward soon.

Now, that double change from Liverpool is here. Barcola and Isak depart to large applause, with Ngumoha and Koumas cheered on as they run onto the pitch.

As expected, Rutter is on. He replaces Ayari, who will think back to his missed chance and shot off the post in the first half.

Gakpo brilliantly turns Costinha, who pulls the winger back to deservedly pick up a booking. Both sides look to be readying changes, with Ngumoha, Koumas and Rutter poised to enter the action.

Brighton seem to have hit a wall in this second half. They’ve struggled to create chances since the break. Liverpool are working really hard defensively.

Once again, Liverpool break through Gakpo. This time, it comes from a Brighton corner, but Gakpo’s cross for Isak at the back post is read by Dunk.

In his first involvement since entering the action, Nyoni ends a slick Brighton move by taking the ball off De Cuyper’s toe in the penalty area with a much-needed clearance. He seems to be limping after he was caught by De Cuyper.

Wirtz’s game is over and he departs to be replaced by Nyoni in Liverpool’s first change.

After some treatment for Wirtz, Vuskovic eventually takes the free kick. It’s in such an inviting position, but the defender gets too power on his strike and whips it over the bar.

This game is still very much in the balance, even though Liverpool have a two goal advantage, and it speaks volumes about both teams’ commitment to attack. #1238. Barcelona's road back to the top runs through Lamine Yamal and Raphinha, and Aston Villa got a front row seat

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There are normal ways to build up to a marquee UEFA Champions League match and there's Aston Villa, for whom the top searches under Google's news tab were all about being taken seriously. This was hardly an exercise in projecting confidence ahead of a trip to Barcelona; the club picked a fight with a broadcaster instead because, for some reason, they deemed he had the power "to stop our ascension in English and European football." Villa's year-over-year improvements are hard to deny, to the point that being somewhat competitive at the Camp Nou on Tuesday was not out of the question and they managed that much. There was just one problem, though.

Punching above your weight is easier said than done against this version of Barcelona.

Villa were no slouch but over the course of a 3-0 win on Matchday 4 of the Champions League, Barcelona were simply in cruise control. It is not that Villa did not pose a challenge – they sparked at times in the first half, Johan Manzambi responsible for the visitors' best chance of the game around the half-hour mark. There was simply nothing they could do at the Camp Nou, their ascension irrelevant even if it is true, because Barcelona are as close to the summit as it gets.

Barcelona barely put a foot wrong as they strung together a trademark performance, well-positioned to do the easy things when the time called for them. That was true as soon as the seventh minute when Joao Gomes, under very little pressure, played a perfect pass to Lamine Yamal with plenty of space in front of him. Even as a couple of Villa defenders tried to close the space near goal, Yamal found his crevice and finished the chance off. It was perhaps the easiest way for him to score his 14th Champions League goal, surpassing Kylian Mbappe as the teenager with the most goals in the competition.

Lamine stands alone 😤Yamal scores his 14th #UCL goal to become the competition’s all-time leading teenage goalscorer 👏Watch #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/Va8Ks3SEHv

The hosts overwhelmed Villa's defense with ease, Yamal's goal merely the first sign of trouble for the visitors. Raphinha bagged a 12-minute brace in the second half, the entire collection of goals a remarkable example of defensive errors. There's a comedy to the Brazil international's first goal, something casual about his strike despite three Villa defenders in his vicinity, watching the ball as it flew into the back of the net. On his second, Joao Cancelo was essentially given permission to dance around Villa's defense to find a Raphinha that was virtually unmarked and converted again from close range.

Raphinha with a 12-minute brace 💥He has scored 19 goals for Barcelona this season in all competitions 💥 pic.twitter.com/R39J7g9y6M

The mistakes from Villa were glaring, almost obfuscating Barcelona's performance entirely. It was not simply a walk in the park, though – Hansi Flick's side got to roll out Plan A and showcase its strengths fully, the lopsided result reflecting the more subtle elements of their dominance. They were able to possess exactly as they wanted to, taking 16 shots and generating 1.99 expected goals along the way. Their attacking might is hardly a surprise now that Raphinha is several years into a career revitalization steered by Flick and now that Yamal is already well known as the sport's next great talent.

What was more impressive was their ability to completely shut Villa out, especially so considering the circumstances. The game state was not exactly a deterrent to Unai Emery's side – 10 days earlier, they let Manchester City have the ball and took their chances despite posting 0.61 expected goals and notched a 2-1 win in the process. Their total was a little better on Tuesday at Barcelona, generating 0.72 expected goals from nine shots, and this time they had the benefit of playing against an understaffed defense. A series of injuries have plagued Barcelona's back line in recent weeks, stripping a defense of the early season stability that had become a new trademark despite sticking true to the high line.

Villa, though, were unable to make much of a dent. Nicolas Jackson, who had eight goals in 12 games across all competitions before the trip to Barcelona, took just one shot on Tuesday. Any semblance of attacking threat never came through. Rodri was not exactly some great denier, either – the captain of Spain's World Cup-winning team only played the first 45 minutes, earning the right to exit the game early after another job well done. Barcelona ensured Villa were dull over the course of 90 minutes; the defensive mistakes from the visitors were the end product rather than the cause of the hosts' success.

On a day where Villa's ascension was cast aside, Barcelona's rise was hard to miss. The gap they are trying to make up is smaller and easier to envision but it does not mean that Flick's side does not carry a certain amount of baggage on each and every Champions League night. They are 11 years removed from the last time they won Europe's top title, a lengthy stretch for one of the game's most celebrated teams. Self-imposed financial hardship has hindered their progress but since Flick took the job two years ago, they have inched closer and closer to the winner's medals they have been eager to collect.

Beating Paris Saint-Germain, the undeniable favorites after back-to-back titles, to the podium is another question entirely, especially after a 4-2 loss in the French capital on Matchday 3. Flick, though, insisted that day was merely a step on the journey, an experience to learn from as they attempt to ascend up Europe's ranks themselves. Champions often make their case on difficult days and should Barcelona make a deep run, they will likely have the chance to do just that down the stretch. The road to the Champions League title, though, usually includes some impressively unfussy days and on Tuesday, Flick's side collected one.

#1237. Pocognoli fears Scottish Premiership 'identity crisis' over lack of homegrown stars

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 17:55 EST, 11 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli believes the Premiership has an identity crisis caused by a lack of Scottish players pulling on the jersey at our top clubs.

Just six of the 26 players the newly appointed national team manager initially selected for the Nations League double-header with North Macedonia and Switzerland play their football in this country’s top division.

And while the Belgian understands the attraction and the benefits of top talents moving to some of Europe’s top leagues, he’s concerned that the division which should be his first port of call when it comes to making selections is now a barren land.

‘The Scottish league misses Scottish players in the biggest teams,’ he said.

‘The league is intense and competitive, but I am not looking at this. I am looking at who is performing at the big clubs.

‘I believe that’s the most close to international level. And for that you need to play Champions League, Europa League, Conference League in some stage of the competition.

‘That is what I’m looking at. I hope that players who are performing well, let’s say in the bottom (half), can bounce to the next step to a top club inside the country.

Pocognoli has been alarmed by the lack of Scottish talent in the SPFL Premiership

Pocognoli has been impressed by the progress of young Celtic full-back Colby Donovan

‘That will make the competition more competitive, maybe you will go through after the winter into the Champions League or Europa League.

‘That gives the experience to the young Scottish players and in the end, we’d get the benefit.

‘That’s what I’m looking at more in Scottish football rather than the clubs and the style of play of clubs, that kind of thing.

‘It’s not easy because if you look at the Scottish competition, there’s not many young lads who are getting an opportunity to shine compared to Belgium, France, Germany.’

The specific issue of a lack of opportunities being afforded to players who are eligible for the Scotland under 21 side was highlighted at the recent summit at St Andrews which all 42 clubs attended.

With Turkey the only nation which currently gives fewer minutes, the SFA’s chief football officer Craig Mulholland has tabled two proposals which would see clubs obliged to offer more chances to emerging talents in both league and cup matches.

Optimistic that such changes to the rules would lead to a brighter picture further down the line, Pocognoli added: ‘Hopefully, we can see the benefits in future.

‘I follow all of the young lads, not only from the Premiership in Scotland, but also the Championship and League One because some of them are on loan.

‘My job is not only to win the next game, it’s also to prepare for what’s coming next season.

‘In one year, a lot can change. I try to support all the decisions of the clubs in Scotland regarding the fact they play Scottish players and young ones especially.

‘Colby Donovan is a good example, he played some good games for Celtic and I tried to help to accelerate his progress, then he signed a new contract and plays week after week.

‘He is not selected this time, but I think we will get the benefit later on.

‘For Findlay Curtis it’s the same, he’s not playing a lot at Rangers but I believe in his quality.

‘We need to support those type of players because we need them, but hopefully it can help his pathway at Rangers to get some minutes.

‘I hope some other players will be on the same pathway this season.’

#1236. Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

#1235. Viking's UCL journey and the rise of co-head coaches: Why two managers might be better than one

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Are two coaches better than one? This is a question that teams around the world, like Viking FK, are trying to answer as they bring dual head coaches to the big stage in Champions League play. The Norwegian side aren't alone in their exploits, as Lyngby in Denmark and Lincoln City in the English Championship are a few of the clubs to join in employing dual head coaches, but they're among the most notable, as Morten Jensen and Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim were able to lead the club to a 3-3 draw with Bayern Munich in Champions League play. There may just be a method to the madness.

Viking were trailblazers on the pitch, appointing the duo in 2020, and they helped lead the club to their first Norwegian league title in 34 years, which sent them into the Champions League for this campaign. Jensen and Aarsheim had chances to interview for the role, but being good friends off the pitch, they suggested taking it on together, a situation that the club has no regrets about as they add to the improving stature of Norwegian soccer.

"When the former coach left us, we knew we needed another coach, and we started the interview process. We brought the two assistant coaches in for different interviews, and then when the interview came, they just showed up together," club CEO Eirik Bjorno said, reminiscing on how this came to be to CBS Sports Golazo in September. "It was their idea. We said we needed to pick one of you, and they said that they were going to do it together. At the end, we said, 'Let's do it.' It has been fairly successful so far; there is no difference between them. They are both head coaches. It's fascinating when we have discussions: I discuss one thing with one of them, and then another thing with the other one, and then we sit down all together to find a solution. I just created more work for myself; I don't recommend it, to be honest."

But while they took a route of forcing the club's hand due to their own relationship and wanting to work together, that's not the only way for this to come to be. At Lyngby, the club wanted to install a dual setup when their manager, Morten Karlsen, was fired in December of 2025. Andreas Bjelland was already at the club as an assistant but had never held a head coaching role. When Mikkel Jespersen was recently let go from Mainz, the club reached out. As Jespersen described it, "We talked about life, football, everything just to see if there was a connection, and luckily there was, and we took it from there step by step, and we jumped into the cooperation."

Bjelland echoes how important it was for those meetings to go well before they jumped into managing Lyngby.

"Because you have to work really closely, it also has to be a person that you work quite well with and can understand and talk to in all kinds of different matters in life," Bjelland said. "So the meetings leading up to the co-coaching were the thing that gave the right feeling."

The duo may not be breaking down the door for the Champions League yet, but their leadership led the club to promotion back to the Danish Superliga, Denmark's top flight, while they're also helping shape the future of American soccer, as USMNT international Neil Pierre was part of the promotion-winning setup and Diego Kochen is currently the starting keeper for the club while on loan from Barcelona. The club hasn't won the Superliga since the 1991-92 season, so their path mirrors an early stage of Viking's, where the immediate goal is steady improvement in order to establish themselves back in the top flight, and the teamwork that Jespersen and Bjelland bring to the club makes them well positioned to do so.

"We're quite different. I think that's one of the things as well that really makes a good team, is that as persons we're quite different and how we act in front of the players, our personalities and all that stuff," Bjelland says. "A little bit like a relationship that you have to be different than your partner, else it wouldn't work. And that's for me a little bit the same, even though we don't hug and kiss. We still have to know a lot about each other, but being different is also a big thing about it that gives us all the tools that we have, so that we can cover more."

Differences in management are what bring a major challenge to balancing these roles. Bjorno spoke about needing to meet with both coaches about the same topics at Viking, and they've also opened up about how they need to work through disagreements when it comes to coaching decisions. You can't go out to the squad with one coach wanting to go in one direction while the other wants to go in the opposite, and that level of conflict resolution is something that these clubs go through behind closed doors ahead of time.

"Then we'll discuss, loudly sometimes, with the rest of our staff in the coaching room, and we will both have to defend our choices and reasoning to them," Jensen said in an interview with the Guardian. "We'll all discuss it until we have an agreement. But 99% of the time, we are pretty agreed in terms of who to use in a particular game, so it's very seldom we waste time over that."

Aarsheim added, "I can read Morten in one second. If he really wants something from his stomach, then I sense it: 'OK, let's go with that.' It's never been a problem."

It's similar at Lyngby, where the coaches have created a structure between themselves.

"We need to be really aligned in everything we do, and then the roles have to be really clear," Bjelland said. "So every day we know exactly who's doing what. So Mikkel has a lot of the things against the ball on minus three, and then I would have on the ball minus two. So everything we do is really structured. Of course, we discuss everything, and it takes some extra talks, and it takes some extra work to do, so we have to be pretty aligned in everything that we say and do."

The trust to know that a coach is saying what you'd expect when meeting with players is something that's built through working together, and when done well, it can make the job easier for those involved because you have someone to brainstorm with and work on tactical decisions with. In life, it's natural to have someone who can be a sounding board, and while assistant coaches can do that too, it's a different power dynamic than when someone is in the same position as you as a head coach.

"Yeah, it is. Especially when it's the first time both of us are head coaches," Jespersen said on the comfort of having a dual manager in charge with him. "It's nice to have each other to talk everything through. Also, when you're in doubt, it's nice to have someone who maybe has the same doubts as you to make the right decision."

It takes a particular style of group to make it work, but these clubs are using it with success, and it could be something that others try to emulate. Watching Viking perform and manage this at the highest level, others have already followed, with Lyngby and Lincoln City moving in the dual head coach direction in the past year. If that continues to catch on,  we may be seeing the buds of a new coaching revolution in the global game.

#1234. What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Liverpool's attack in need of jump start

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Champions League reaches its midpoint Wednesday night and if the last few rounds of fixtures are anything to go off, it will do so amid a hailstorm of goals. Wouldn't that be good news for Liverpool, even though their Champions League scoring record is already more impressive than in the Premier League? Meanwhile, there are plenty of high-stakes matchups at each end of the table. Real Betis are one of only four teams still standing with a 100% record but that could well be tested on the road against Borussia Dortmund.

At the other end of the table, Porto have a lot of work to do. Marooned in 35th, only the Portuguese league leaders and Slovan Bratislava are yet to get among the points. Surely if they do not do something tonight against Napoli, their competition will be done, right?

All that, plus Real Madrid, Arsenal and Manchester City in action tonight. It's sure to be a busy day.

If all you had to assess a team on from the season so far was the league phase table, you would believe that Liverpool are as advertised. That half a billion or so they have spent on their attack since the start of last season seems to be well spent, 12 goals from their first three Champions League games as Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Dominik Szoboszlai share in the scoring. Andoni Iraola's side may look a little vulnerable at the other end, but if you look at the talent in the Reds' roster, you score three, we'll score four-ball seems a pretty shrewd use of talent.

And yet the free-scoring Liverpool of the Champions League have been hard to spot in their domestic games. With the caveat that most teams' numbers take a dink after they run into Arsenal, at the nine-game mark in the Premier League season Liverpool have just 11 goals to their name. Only some of that can be accounted for through poor finishing -- Szoboszlai, Wirtz, Barcola and Cody Gakpo have two Premier League goals off 5.24 xG -- and the bigger issue is that this team ranks 11th in the league for expected goals.

As the graphic above indicates, there are quite widespread issues with the quality of shots Liverpool are settling for. Across Europe's top five leagues, the xG value of the average shot this season is 0.111. In no context do Iraola's team get particularly close to that mark. Instead, they take a lot of shots from outside the box, just under 40%, and they lead Europe's top five leagues for the proportion of their shots that are blocked, 37.9%.

Curiously low-quality shots were not exactly an issue that bedevilled Iraola's previous team. Last season Bournemouth ranked quite highly in terms of xG per shot both from open play and dead balls. A sign of a team that was humming as a unit and had grasped how the coach wanted to turn the chaos they engendered into quality scoring chances? Iraola will hope so. That augurs better for Liverpool than the possibility that the talents in which so much has been invested just don't quite gel.

That Liverpool's numbers are different in the Champions League might be telling us little more than the fact that their last two games in particular -- away to LASK, at home to Villarreal -- have been fairly favorable to run up the goals. The 12 they have scored have come off 7.23 worth of xG and a quarter of their shots are being blocked. You would not, then, want to get carried away with the idea that this is a team who will just be able to flick a switch when the Champions League music starts playing in Istanbul on Wednesday night.

Defeat at home to Napoli would not actually be critical to Porto's hopes of advancing to the knockout round of the Champions League. De facto, however? Yeah, probably. If projection models and past seasons are anything to go on, nine points is a decent guide to where the cut line will land after eight games. You do not want to have to accrue all of them after the turn. After all, Porto don't really have three gimmes left after the international break. You'd fancy Francesco Farioli's side to beat Slavia Prague away and LASK at home but their other games are on the road. Feyenoord could be tough, Liverpool would be.

Porto might reasonably feel they could have got more from these games. The first half against Manchester City was played even and there were half openings before Erling Haaland's late goal. Real Betis also did for them late on, two goals in the final 16 minutes earning the La Liga side a win in Seville while PSV beat them with perhaps the game's only clear opening last time out. That last line speaks to the issue that will have to be resolved over the next five games. Porto just do not take enough shots.

Thirty of them worth a combined 2.7 xG just is not going to cut it for a team who are averaging not far off that number per game in domestic competition. Strikers Samu Aghehowa and Andre Silva have just four shots between them. Domestically, this is a team that does supplement their output from center forward with more attempts from deeper but Gabri Veiga has just five shots to his name. Borja Sainz averages nearly three and a half in the Primeira Liga. He is yet to take a shot in the Champions League. This looks like the familiar story of a Portuguese team dominating 15 dramatically inferior opponents at home and struggling when the difficulty level ramps up in Europe.

"The Champions League is a different competition," said Farioli. "The demands and the details make all the difference. Being effective at every moment is important, as we've seen in the first three matches.

"I hope experience helps us be more effective than we have been. In terms of performances, we're doing well, but we can do more, because this isn't enough. We're working to raise our level, and tomorrow is the moment to do that and claim the points we want so much."

Fail to do so and that might effectively be it for Porto and this season's Champions League.

One might discount a player who has scored 40 goals in his last 71 league games for Borussia Dortmund with the two most devastating words in the footballing lexicon: Bundesliga tax. And you know what, sometimes those words cut through because there is truth to them. I fear that may be the case for a certain F. Wirtz.

Serhou Guirassy, though? Well, right now he is finding ways to score in every competition. A poacher's finish from his only shot helped earn Dortmund a backs-to-the-wall 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich, setting him up nicely for his return to a competition where he has excelled for a number of years. In 31 Champions League games, four for Rennes and the rest in Dortmund colors, the 30-year-old has 23 goals. Admittedly, seven of those are penalties but a goal every other game at the highest level of club football is not to be sniffed at. Nor are 0.63 non-penalty expected goals per 90 minutes.

Notably, Guirassy has enjoyed some of his greatest success against Spanish opposition, scoring in each encounter, a hat trick against Barcelona in 2025, perhaps his best moment. It might be that the Guinean striker is just an archetype that the best of La Liga do not face that often. At 6ft 2in, Guirassy is big, strong and impressively mobile, at least when his opponents aren't the big, hulking center backs of Chelsea and Manchester City. Could he have baited the same penalty off them that he got against Villarreal back in September? Certainly you wouldn't fancy him to have quite the same bully ball joy off set pieces that he did against Villarreal, Athletic Club and Barcelona.

As for Wednesday's opponent, it might be tricky for Real Betis. It's worth saying that in their three Champions League games so far they have allowed just over 2.5 xG against good opposition: Lille, Porto and Feyenoord. In La Liga, however, they rank 18th for set piece xG allowed and set piece goals conceded. They're not particularly great at limiting touches and xG in the box either. This could be another banner day for Guirassy.

#1232. UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressive and fatal neurodegenerative condition. Recently, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting SOD1 and FUS have shown early promise in clinical trials9,10, but these approaches only benefit patients with SOD1 and FUS mutations—less than 3% of patients with ALS—leaving an urgent need for therapies for the remaining roughly 97% of patients with ALS. A common feature of all non-FUS and non-SOD1 ALS is the aggregation of TAR DNA binding protein-43 (TDP-43) in neurons1,2, a finding also observed in roughly 50% of both frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer’s disease2,11. However, no therapies that directly target TDP-43 are available, leaving the underlying nuclear loss of function (LoF) unaddressed. TDP-43 is an RNA-binding protein that is normally located in the nucleus and has crucial roles in the regulation of RNA splicing12,13. Cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 induces a nuclear LoF resulting in cryptic exon inclusion, cryptic alternative polyadenylation and/or exon skipping in some mature messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts3. These events occur in hundreds of transcripts, including genes with crucial neuronal functions, such as STMN2, UNC13A and KCNQ2 (refs. 4,5,6,7,8). Whereas the impact of STMN2 mis-splicing on axonal regeneration and KCNQ2 exon skipping on intrinsic excitability has been studied, the direct impact of TDP-43 LoF on synaptic function has not been addressed.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have shown that single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within and proximal to a cryptic exon in UNC13A increase the risk of developing ALS and accelerate disease progression14,15,16. Under normal physiological conditions, these risk SNPs do not induce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, but after TDP-43 LoF, risk SNPs exacerbate cryptic exon inclusion leading to increased loss of functional RNA transcripts and protein6,7. UNC13A is a presynaptic protein that is required at the active zone to properly dock and prime synaptic vesicles for fusion with the plasma membrane17. Genetic deletion of Unc13a in mice leads to a roughly 90% reduction in spontaneous and evoked glutamatergic excitatory synaptic transmission18,19,20. Although the UNC13A genetic association strongly implicates this event in ALS pathogenesis, the contribution of TDP-43 LoF to synaptic dysfunction and the role of UNC13A cryptic splicing—particularly in the context of many mis-splicing events in other synaptic transcripts—is unaddressed. Resolving these outstanding questions is crucial for establishing whether correcting UNC13A splicing represents a viable therapeutic approach for restoring normal neuronal function.

Here we report that TDP-43 loss in mature human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell-derived neurons induces loss of presynaptic UNC13A and a notable reduction in AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) receptor-mediated synaptic transmission, leading to a loss of coordinated network activity. Despite the widespread roles of TDP-43 in RNA regulation, isolated genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon rescues these deficits, demonstrating that this single event is a key driver of synapse dysfunction in ALS. To this end, we developed splice-switching ASOs that can rescue UNC13A mRNA splicing, UNC13A protein levels and UNC13A presynaptic localization, and restore both spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ASO treatment rescues UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion in a humanized mouse model that recreates this human-specific mis-splicing event. Thus, ASOs targeting the UNC13A cryptic exon represent an innovative therapeutic strategy for treating ALS and FTD, and their use for treating sporadic ALS is supported by genetic evidence.

TDP-43 plays important roles in development and therefore, to avoid interfering with neuronal maturation by depleting TDP-43 from the iPS cell stage, we used CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to generate a cell line in which both endogenous copies of TDP-43 harbour a HaloTag to allow for proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC)-mediated21 knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a–d). TDP-43 is degraded by HaloPROTAC in a dose-dependent manner and in a process blocked by proteasome inhibition or the NEDD8 E1 inhibitor (Extended Data Fig. 1e–g). HaloTag-TDP-43 iPS cells were differentiated into mature excitatory cortical-like neurons (HaloTDP iNeurons) that expressed the layer V excitatory cortical marker CTIP2 and lacked expression of the inhibitory marker NKX2.1 or the neuronal progenitor marker PAX6 (Extended Data Fig. 1h). TDP-43 was also found to be correctly localized to the nucleus (Fig. 1b). Tagging of TDP-43 can alter its function and, whereas the HaloTag partially affected TDP-43 function (Extended Data Fig. 1i), UNC13A cryptic splicing and mRNA downregulation were robustly detected only on HaloPROTAC knockdown of TDP-43 (Fig. 1c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2a), similar to CRISPR interference (CRISPRi)-mediated knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 2b–f). Loss of UNC13A mRNA led to a time-dependent decrease in UNC13A protein whereby less than 5% of protein remained after 10 days of HaloPROTAC treatment (Fig. 1e,f). Immunofluorescence staining revealed a loss of synaptic UNC13A staining at synapsin-positive puncta (Fig. 1g,h). HaloPROTAC-mediated knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons did not lead to alterations in the RNA levels of N-methyl-d-aspartate and AMPA receptor subunits as assessed by reverse transcription–quantitative PCR (RT–qPCR) (Extended Data Fig. 2g).

CTRL, control; DIV, days in vitro; FC, fold change; KD, knockdown; NS, not significant; NT, no treatment; PSI, percentage spliced in.

Previous investigations of the physiological functions of UNC13A have been mainly conducted using primary rodent neurons with limited studies in human neurons18,19,20,22. We therefore sought to assess the impact of UNC13A loss in human iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Whole-cell patch clamp recordings showed that depletion of UNC13A through CRISPRi impaired synaptic transmission, as evidenced by a reduction in the frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) (Fig. 1i), consistent with a presynaptic deficit and in line with previously published work19,20. HaloPROTAC-mediated TDP-43 depletion also reduced mEPSC frequency (Fig. 1j), mirroring the presynaptic deficit observed on UNC13A loss. Treatment with 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) blocked mEPSCs, confirming that synaptic events were mediated primarily by means of fast AMPA receptor-mediated glutamatergic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Whereas UNC13A depletion had no effect on mEPSC amplitude, consistent with a purely presynaptic deficit (Extended Data Fig. 3b), TDP-43 depletion led to a modest reduction in amplitude (Extended Data Fig. 3c), suggesting extra postsynaptic deficits independent of UNC13A depletion. Passive membrane properties remained comparable between control and UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e).

To investigate the effect of UNC13A and TDP-43 loss on network activity, we carried out multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings. We found that either UNC13A or TDP-43 depletion induced a disordered and asynchronous pattern of network activity, measured by a reduction in the normalized electrode cross-correlations (Fig. 1k–m). This result indicates that UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons fail to support network-level activity. The number of active electrodes remained consistent (Extended Data Fig. 3g) and phase-contrast images showed comparable cell coverage between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3h), ruling out issues with electrode coverage as a confounding factor. CNQX treatment of control neurons confirmed network synchrony was highly dependent on fast AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Whereas extra MEA metrics were also affected by both TDP-43 and UNC13A loss, the network synchrony deficit was the largest and most consistently observed change (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Thus, we show that TDP-43 depletion substantially impairs fast glutamatergic synaptic transmission and synchronized network activity in human neurons, mirroring a comparable loss of synaptic function and network activity induced by direct UNC13A loss.

Knockdown of TDP-43 leads to cryptic exon inclusion within UNC13A intron 20 along with an independent downstream intron retention event at intron 31 and other lower-frequency splicing abnormalities throughout the UNC13A mRNA transcript6,7. To determine the degree to which protein loss is dependent on the UNC13A intron 20 cryptic exon, we performed CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing to remove the cryptic exon from the genome of SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Using two single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) we made a homozygous deletion of 233 nucleotides (nt) that contain both splice acceptors and the common donor splice site of the cryptic exon. In wild-type (WT) cells containing the full UNC13A gene there was robust induction of UNC13A mis-splicing after TDP-43 depletion as assessed by reverse transcription–PCR (RT–PCR) (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d), whereas in cells with genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, no cryptic splicing was detected (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Cryptic exon deletion rescued correctly spliced levels of UNC13A mRNA, as determined by RT–qPCR, and led to roughly 75% rescue of UNC13A protein following TDP-43 knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 4e–g). We subsequently deleted the UNC13A cryptic exon in iPS cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a–e) and detected a similar rescue in UNC13A RNA and protein following CRISPRi-mediated knockdown of TDP-43, confirming the relevance of this event in iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 5f–k). In the UNC13A cryptic exon deletion cell line, we performed further CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to add a HaloTag in the TARDBP gene to efficiently induce TDP-43 loss after differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 6). Similar to results in SH-SY5Y cells, genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in HaloTDP iNeurons rescued UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction and restored mRNA and presynaptic protein levels (Fig. 2a–h), demonstrating this splicing event is the main driver of TDP-43-dependent UNC13A loss.

a, Schematic of genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon (CE). b–f, Analysis of WT and CE deletion (CE DEL) HaloTDP iNeurons on DIV28 following 14 days of HaloPROTAC treatment. b, RT–PCR showing that CE DEL restores UNC13A exon 20–21 splicing after TDP-43 knockdown. c, Quantification of b; n = 6 biological replicates from 3 experiments. d, RT–qPCR of correctly spliced UNC13A showing rescued RNA levels after TDP-43 knockdown; n = 6 biological replicates from 3 experiments. e, Western blot showing rescue of UNC13A protein levels by CE DEL. f, Quantification of e; n = 6 biological replicates from 3 experiments. g, Synapsin and UNC13A immunofluorescence in 4-week-old HaloTDP and CE DEL iNeurons cultured on rat astrocytes after 2 weeks of TDP-43 knockdown. h, UNC13A intensity at synapsin-positive terminals (control n = 71; TDP-43 knockdown n = 71; cryptic exon Del n = 66; CE DEL + TDP-43 knockdown n = 75 synapses; 3 experiments). i, Representative and mean mEPSC traces. j, mEPSC frequency and inter-event interval cumulative distributions (control n = 17; TDP-43 knockdown n = 22; CE DEL n = 15; CE DEL + TDP-43 knockdown n = 28 iNeurons; 3 experiments). k, Representative DIV39 MEA raster plots (60 s) for control, TDP-43 knockdown, CE DEL and CE DEL + TDP-43 knockdown; electrode bursts, blue; network bursts, pink. l, Network synchrony following TDP-43 knockdown, expressed as log2[fold change] in normalized electrode cross-correlation (n = 4 independent experiments); lines connect parallel differentiations recorded on the same MEA plate. Statistics: one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s test (c,d); repeated-measures one-way ANOVA on log-transformed, loading control-normalized values with Tukey’s test (f); Gaussian LMM with two-sided Satterthwaite-corrected t-tests (h,j); two-sided paired ratio t-test (l). *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.001; ****P < 0.0001. Scale bar, 10 µm. gRNA, guide RNA. Uncropped gels are shown in Supplementary Fig. 2.

TDP-43 knockdown yields synaptic transmission defects similar to those induced by direct depletion of UNC13A. However, TDP-43 has hundreds of validated RNA targets, regulating splicing, stability and transport of transcripts involved in virtually every aspect of neuronal function. Therefore, the reduction in synaptic transmission could reflect a multi-gene insult affecting pathways including synaptic vesicle trafficking, Ca2+ signalling and active zone organization. To determine the extent to which UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion contributes to impaired synaptic function following loss of TDP-43, we performed whole-cell patch clamping experiments in WT and cryptic exon deletion lines. Rescue of this single cryptic exon largely restored synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion with an 80% recovery in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 2i,j). mEPSC amplitude was still marginally (roughly 10%) reduced, supporting the conclusion that UNC13A cryptic exon deletion rescues specifically presynaptic function (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Passive membrane properties were similar between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7b). As mEPSC frequency is influenced by synapse number, we measured excitatory synapse density along the dendrites of iNeurons. We found that TDP-43-knockdown neurons had fewer synapses than controls, a feature that persisted even when the UNC13A cryptic exon was deleted (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d), suggesting a strong recovery in synapse function in the remaining synapses.

Despite the small reduction in synapse number, MEA recordings showed that deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in TDP-43-depleted neurons restored synchronous network activity, indicating effective neurotransmitter release and propagation of signalling across the network (Fig. 2k,l and Extended Data Fig. 7e). This represented the most robustly rescued MEA metric (Extended Data Fig. 7f). Taken together, these findings show that correction of a single cryptic exon splicing event (intron 20 UNC13A cryptic exon) is sufficient to restore synaptic transmission and rescue the asynchronous patterns of network activity caused by TDP-43 loss. Active electrodes and cell coverage were comparable across conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Likewise, analysis of neuronal survival confirmed that network-level changes were not attributable to changes in viability due to TDP-43 loss (Extended Data Fig. 7h) demonstrating that TDP-43 driven UNC13A loss drives a functional synaptic deficit in otherwise structurally intact, viable neurons.

The rescue of UNC13A levels and restoration of synaptic signalling conferred by deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in the context of TDP-43 knockdown highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting this event in patients. We therefore sought to identify ASOs that can induce splice switching similar to those successful in targeting splicing events in SMN2 and STMN2 (refs. 23,24). We first designed locked nucleic acid-modified ASOs that targeted regions covering the cryptic exon acceptor and donor splice sites (Extended Data Fig. 8a). We screened the ASOs by transfection in SK-N-BE(2) cells and assessed their ability to restore UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 8b) and found that 21-nt ASOs targeting the donor splice site could restore UNC13A splicing. We confirmed splicing rescue and ability to restore UNC13A RNA and UNC13A protein levels in SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 8c–g). To improve therapeutic tolerance, we adapted the best performing ASOs to have full 2′-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) ribose-modified bases and tested their ability to rescue UNC13A splicing and restore protein levels in HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 8h). We found these could restore splicing to more than 90% and protein levels to 30–50% of normal levels. Treatment with the M21-4 MOE ASO led to increased presynaptic UNC13A protein expression at synapsin-positive puncta following TDP-43 depletion compared with treatment with the control scrambled ASO (Fig. 3d). To identify ASOs that could increase protein rescue above 50% of normal levels, we carried out a secondary screen by performing an ASO walk along the cryptic donor site with 18-nt MOE-based ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 9a). We evaluated the ability of the 18-nt ASOs to rescue splicing in SH-SY5Y cells by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 9b) and confirmed that the best performing 18-nt ASOs could rescue correct UNC13A mRNA splicing to more than 90%, and protein to more than 50% in SH-SY5Y cells and HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 9c–h). In addition, we performed amplicon sequencing, which confirmed the ability of ASOs to rescue both reference and risk alleles in our HaloTDP iNeurons (Extended Data Fig. 9i).

Illustrations in g adapted from the NIH BioArt Source (https://bioart.niaid.nih.gov/bioart/505).

To validate the efficacy of UNC13A ASOs to rescue cryptic splicing in an in vivo model, we generated humanized UNC13A (hUNC13A) reporter mice, in which mouse intron 20 was replaced with human UNC13A intron 20 containing the cryptic exon. TDP-43 knockdown was performed by tail vein injection of an adeno-associated virus encoding a synthetic microRNA targeting the mouse Tardbp gene (Fig. 3g). On the same day, intracerebroventricular injections were performed in hUNC13A reporter mice with the M21-4 MOE ASO or artificial cerebrospinal fluid. Three weeks post-injection, spinal cords were dissected from the mice. RT–PCR analysis from spinal cord tissue following knockdown of TDP-43 showed no cryptic exon inclusion in WT mice and robust cryptic exon inclusion in hUNC13A reporter mice, which was partially rescued by administration of UNC13A splice-correcting ASO (Fig. 3h–k). Overall, these results show that ASOs can reduce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon on TDP-43 knockdown both in vitro and in vivo, and can rescue UNC13A protein expression to above 50% in cultured neurons.

Unc13a heterozygous knockout mice and individuals with heterozygous LoF UNC13A mutations are viable and do not present with abnormal neurophysiology18,25. Recovery of UNC13A expression to WT levels after TDP-43 LoF is probably not required to restore synapse function, in agreement with previous work in primary mouse cultures that showed that clear deficits in synapse function are only observed when expression of Unc13a falls below 30% of normal physiological levels20,25. Indeed, treatment with M18-17 ASO, which rescues UNC13A levels to more than 50% of control, was able to rescue synaptic transmission as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4a). We then tested our M21-4 ASO, which rescues UNC13A protein levels to roughly 30% of normal levels. Despite the lower level of protein rescue, treatment with M21-4 ASO also rescued synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4b). mEPSC amplitude and passive membrane properties were unaffected by treatment with ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 10a–d), suggesting that ASO treatment specifically rescues presynaptic deficits caused by the cryptic exon in UNC13A.
